(Sūrat al-Qalam is Makkī, and it has fifty-two verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe.﴾ ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for you is a reward never cut off.﴾ ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ ﴿So you will see and they will see.﴾ ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ [al-Qalam: 7] ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ [al-Qalam: 8] ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise.﴾ [al-Qalam: 9] ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-maker.﴾ [al-Qalam: 10] ﴿A defamer, going about with slander.﴾ [al-Qalam: 11] ﴿A hinderer of good, transgressing and sinful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 12] ﴿Brutal, and after that, of illegitimate birth.﴾ [al-Qalam: 13] ﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Myths of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 15] ﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ [al-Qalam: 16] ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest its fruit at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] ﴿and did not make exception.﴾ [al-Qalam: 18] ﴿So there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep.﴾ [al-Qalam: 19] ﴿And it became like the reaped.﴾ [al-Qalam: 20] ﴿So they called to one another at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 21] ﴿"Go early to your field, if you are going to harvest."﴾ [al-Qalam: 22] ﴿So they set out, while whispering to one another,﴾ [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿"No poor man shall enter it today upon you."﴾ [al-Qalam: 24] ﴿And they went early with determination, as those capable.﴾ [al-Qalam: 25] ﴿But when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ [al-Qalam: 26] ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ [al-Qalam: 27] ﴿Said the most moderate of them, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify Allah?'"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28] ﴿They said, "Exalted is our Lord. Indeed, we have been wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Qalam: 29] ﴿Then they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ [al-Qalam: 30] ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we have been transgressors.﴾ [al-Qalam: 31] ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it. Indeed, we turn to our Lord in desire."﴾ [al-Qalam: 32] ﴿Such is the punishment; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ [al-Qalam: 33] ﴿Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ [al-Qalam: 34] ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35] ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a book in which you study,﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿that indeed for you therein is whatever you choose?﴾ [al-Qalam: 38] ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection, that indeed for you is whatever you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that.﴾ [al-Qalam: 40] ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able.﴾ [al-Qalam: 42] ﴿Their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, while they had been called to prostration when they were sound.﴾ [al-Qalam: 43] ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 45] ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Qalam: 46] ﴿Or is the unseen with them, so they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47] ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief].﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿So his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾ [al-Qalam: 50] ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad!"﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] ﴿But it is not except a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]

(p-305) "al-Mahin" (contemptible): al-Rummani said: the lowly, because of his frequent engagement in ugly deeds, from al-mahana, which is lowness. The root meaning of al-hamz in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: and with his eye and his gesture. An-namim and an-namima are both verbal nouns of (namma), which is conveying what one hears of that which is hurtful and stirs up souls. It was also said: an-namim is the plural of namima, meaning by it the generic noun. Al-'utull: al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the one fierce in contentiousness with falsehood. Ma'mar said: he is the vile and base. The poet said:
"With a brutal man among men, of illegitimate birth, neither courageous nor noble."
It was also said: the one who drags people, i.e., drags them to prison or punishment; and from it: "Seize him and drag him" (khudhuhu fa'tiluhu). Ibn al-Sikkit said: I dragged him ('ataltuhu) and 'atantuhu, with lam and nun. Az-zanim: the pretender (ad-da'iy). Hassan said:
"An illegitimate one, whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the hide's width."
(And he also said):
"You are an illegitimate one, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."
Az-zanim is from az-zamana, which is a piece of goat's skin that is cut off and left hanging from a ring. The pretender was named so because he is an added appendage attached to other than his own people. Wasamahu: he made a mark on him, which is a sign pointing to something. Jarir said:
"When I placed my branding on al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith I slit the nose of al-Akhtal."
Al-Khurtum: the nose; and al-khurtum is one of the attributes of wine. The poet said:
"I have witnessed among them a drinking gathering with a zamir-player, while the people are struck down by a foaming, pale wine."
Ash-Shamantari said: al-khurtum is the first of its flowing out from the jar, and it is also called the nose, for that is its purest and finest. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-khurtum is wine, and he recited for al-A'raj al-Mughanni:
"You spend your day in amusement and play, while at night you are a drinker of the khara'im."
As-Sirram: the gathering of date-palms. Al-Harad: prevention, from their saying: harathat al-ibil, when its milk diminished; and harathat as-sanah, when its rain and goodness diminished, as Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi said; and al-harad is anger. Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim, the companion of al-Asma'i, said: it is lightened (mukhaffaf), and he recited:
"When the steeds come charging, filled with anger and harad."
(And al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said):
"Lions of a thicket met lions unseen, pouring for one another, upon harad, the blood of lions."
Ibn al-Sikkit said: it may be vocalized with a kasra: one says harida, bi'l-kasr, haradan, so he is haradan, and from it it is said: a hared lion, and hawarid lions. Al-harad is also isolation: harada yahridu huruden: he withdrew from his people and descended alone, not mixing with them; and a harud star is one separated from the stars. Al-Asma'i said: al-munharid is the solitary, in the dialect of Hudhayl. End. Al-harad is also intent: harada yahridu, with kasra: he intended; and from it: haradtu hardaka, i.e., I intended your intent. From it is the poet's saying:
"A torrent came from the command of Allah, heading straight as the walled garden."

(p-306) [Repetition of the verses 1–33 as in the source.]

(p-307) This surah is Makkī. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement about it among any of the people of interpretation. End. Most of it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Abu Jahl. Its connection to what precedes it: in the previous surah He mentioned matters of the state of the blessed and the wretched, and mentioned His overwhelming power and His vast knowledge, and that He, exalted is He, had He willed, would have caused the earth to swallow them or sent upon them a violent wind. What He, exalted is He, informed of was what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received by revelation, while the disbelievers attributed it sometimes to poetry, sometimes to sorcery, and sometimes to madness. So He, glorified and exalted, began this surah by clearing him of what they attributed to him of madness, and by magnifying his reward for his patience upon their harm, and by praising his tremendous character.

(Nūn): a letter of the alphabet, like "Ṣād" and "Qāf", and it is not inflected, like some letters that came with other letters unaffected by governing words. Judging the place of its i'rab is conjecture. What is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it is the name of the great fish upon which the seven earths rest. From Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak: it is the name of the inkwell. From Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, raising it: it is a tablet of light. From Ibn 'Abbas also: it is the last letter of the name al-Rahman. From Ja'far al-Sadiq: it is a river of the rivers of Paradise. Perhaps none of that is sound. Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: "Nūn" is a letter of the alphabet; had it been a complete word it would be inflected as al-qalam is inflected; so it is a letter of spelling, as in all the openings of the surahs. End. Whoever said it is the name of the inkwell or the fish, and claimed it is sworn by like the pen, then if it is a proper noun it should be in the genitive; if feminine it would be non-declined, or if masculine it would be declined; and if it is a common noun it would be inflected and nunated; and none of that applies, so that view is weak. Ibn 'Atiyya said: if it is a name for the inkwell, then either it is a dialect of some Arabs, or an non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized. The poet said:
"When longing for them presses me, the tears of the nun pour forth."
Whoever makes it the Bahamut makes the pen the one that Allah created and commanded to write the creatures, and makes the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to the angels. Whoever says it is a name takes it as the common pen in people's hands. Ibn 'Abbas stated this, and made the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to people, so the oath falls upon this collection: the matter of the Book, which is the foundation of the sciences and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, for the pen is the brother of the tongue and a general blessing from Allah. End. The majority read (Nūn) with a sukūn on the nūn and its idgham into the waw of (wal-qalam) with ghunna, and some people without ghunna; Hamza, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Qalun and Hafs made it clear (izhar). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on the nūn because of the meeting of two sākins. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a fatḥa; this may be a case-ending, and it is a name of the surah sworn by, the preposition is elided so it is in the accusative, not declined due to being a proper noun and feminine, and (wal-qalam) would be conjoined to it. It may also be for the meeting of two sākins, and fatḥa is preferred for lightness, like ayna. (Mā) may be relative or verbal (maṣdariyya). The pronoun in (yasturuna) refers to the scribes, since the pen indicates them; either it means the Recording Angels, or every writer. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by the pen is meant its owners, so the pronoun in (yasturuna) is for them, as if it were said: and the owners of the pen and what they inscribe, or their inscribing. End. This is like His saying: ﴿like darknesses in a deep sea﴾ [al-Nur: 40], meaning "like those of darknesses"; for this reason the pronoun returned to it in His saying: "covered by a wave."

The answer to the oath is: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ It appears that "by the grace of your Lord" is an oath inserted as a parenthesis between the subject and the predicate, for emphasis, to strengthen the assertion, and to stress the complete negation of the blameworthy attribute from him (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Bi-ni'mati Rabbika* (by the grace of your Lord) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), as when you say to someone, 'You are, by the praise of God, excellent.'" End of quote. He did not specify what the *bā'* in *bi-ni'mati* is connected to.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*Bi-majnūnin* (with 'madman') is connected to it in negated form, just as *bi-'āqilin* (with 'sane') is connected in affirmed form in your saying, 'You are, by the grace of God, sane.' Negation and affirmation are equal in this, just as their equality in your saying, 'Zayd struck 'Amr' and 'Zayd did not strike 'Amr', where you govern the verb in the affirmed and negated forms in one and the same way. Its place is the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), as if he had said: 'You are not a madman, having been favoured by that.' The *bā'* does not prevent *majnūn* from governing what precedes it, because it is extra (*zā'idah*) for emphasizing the negation. The meaning is: a dismissal of what the disbelievers of Makkah attributed to him out of enmity and envy, and that it is part of God's favour upon him, through soundness of intellect and the nobility that befits his qualification for prophethood, in its rank." End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari held, that *bi-ni'mati Rabbika* is connected to *majnūn* and is in the position of a *ḥāl*, requires reflection. When negation applies to a predicate that has a complement, there are two ways of reading it. The first is that the negation applies only to that complement. The second is that the negation applies to the predicate itself, so the complement is negated along with it. To illustrate: when you say, "Zayd is not standing hurriedly" (*mā Zaydun qā'imun musri'an*), the mind immediately takes it that his hurrying is negated but not his standing, so he has stood without hurrying. The other reading is that his standing is negated, and therefore his hurrying is negated too, meaning: there is no standing, so there is no hurrying. The position we have established does not allow al-Zamakhshari's view in any way. Rather, it leads to something that may not be said about the infallible (ﷺ).

It was also said: the meaning is "You are not a madman, and the grace is from your Lord," as in their saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You" (*wa-bi-ḥamdika*), meaning "and the praise is to God." From this is the verse of Labid:

*Wa-ufridtu fi'l-dunyā bi-faqdi 'ashīratī*
*wa-fāraqanī jārun bi-Arbada nāfi'u*

Meaning: "And he (the neighbour) is Arbad." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of *i'rāb* (grammatical analysis).

In *al-Muntakhab* there is a summary of the following: the meaning is that madness was removed from you by the grace of your Lord, that is, the presence of the praiseworthy attribute and the removal of the blameworthy attribute through the bounty of your Lord. Then he established by this claim what amounts to a conclusive proof of its truth, because his blessings were manifest in him: perfect eloquence, intellect, a pleasing conduct, freedom from every defect, and the attainment of every noble quality. So the existence and manifestation of these qualities serves as a certainty that they are lying in their claim that he is mad. "And indeed for you there is a reward that will not end" (*wa-inna laka la-ajran*) is for your bearing their slander and for calling people to God, so what they say shall not stop you from calling to God. "And indeed you are upon a magnificent character" is an explanation of what preceded, "by the grace of your Lord," and a definition for whoever accused him of madness, that he lied and erred, and that one who has such pleasing morals cannot be ascribed madness. The wording indicates superiority and dominance. End of quote.

"And indeed for you there is a reward" means: for what you have borne of the burdens of prophethood, and of their harm, in what they attribute to you, though you are not stained by any of the faults they ascribe. "Not interrupted" (*ghayra mamnūn*) means not cut off. *Mananta al-ḥabl* means "I cut the rope." The poet said:

*Ghubsun kawāsibu lā yumannu ṭa'āmuhā*

meaning: "Grey, predatory birds whose food is not cut off." Mujahid said: "not counted." al-Hasan said: "not tainted by reproach." al-Dahhak said: "without work in return." It was also said: "not measured," which is the meaning of Mujahid's view. al-Zamakhshari said: "Or 'not conferred upon you', because it is a reward you deserve for your deed, and not a gift bestowed at the outset. Only bounties are reproached, not wages for deeds." End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine that human acts and divine justice are rationally determined, associated with the Mu'tazila).

"And indeed you are upon a magnificent character." Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "a magnificent religion; there is no religion more beloved to God than it." 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." 'Ali said: "It is the etiquette of the Qur'an." Qatada said: "It is what he used to enjoin by God's command." It was also said: he was called magnificent because noble qualities were gathered in him: nobility of disposition, purity of nature, a beautiful temperament, and excellence of qualities. Whenever anyone called him, he would say, "Here I am" (*labbayka*). He (ﷺ) said: "God sent me to perfect noble character." He instructed Abu Dharr, saying: "Treat people with good character." From him (ﷺ): "Nothing is placed in the scale heavier than good character." He also said: "The most beloved of you to God are those with the best character."

The apparent connection of *bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn* (which of you is the afflicted one) is to what precedes it. 'Uthman al-Mazini said: "The sentence is complete at His saying '*wa-yubṣirūna*' (and they will see), then he begins with '*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*'." End of quote. Then "*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*" is an interrogative intended to present a choice between two matters. It is known that the judgment is negated of one of them, and the existence (of the truth) specifies it: it is the believer, who is neither afflicted nor has any affliction.

When it is connected to what precedes it, which is the view of the majority, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar said: "The *bā'* is extra, and the meaning is: which of you is the afflicted one?" The *bā'* was added to the subject (mubtada'), as it is added in the phrase *bi-ḥasbika dirhamun*, meaning "your sufficiency is a dirham." al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash said: "The *bā'* is not extra, and *al-maftūn* means 'affliction' (*fitnah*). That is: which of you is it that has the affliction and corruption they called madness?" al-Akhfash also said: "Which of you has been afflicted by affliction?" He omitted the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) and put the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governed noun) in its place. So in his first statement he took *al-maftūn* as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here he kept it as a passive participle and interpreted it by omitting a *muḍāf*. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: "The *bā'* has the meaning of *fī* (in). That is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind?" End of quote. Then the *bā'* is locative, like *Zaydun bi'l-Baṣrah*, meaning "Zayd is in Basra." From this view it appears that the *bā'* in the earlier statement is not locative but causal.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*al-maftūn* means the madman, because he was afflicted (*futina*), that is, tested with madness, or because the Arabs claimed that he was from the delusion of the jinn, and they are the seducers (*al-futtān*) of the seducers among them." End of quote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fī ayyikumu al-maftūn* (in which of you is the afflicted one).

The answer to the oath is: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ It appears that "by the grace of your Lord" is an oath inserted as a parenthesis between the subject and the predicate, for emphasis, to strengthen the assertion, and to stress the complete negation of the blameworthy attribute from him (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Bi-ni'mati Rabbika* (by the grace of your Lord) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), as when you say to someone, 'You are, by the praise of God, excellent.'" End of quote. He did not specify what the *bā'* in *bi-ni'mati* is connected to.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*Bi-majnūnin* (with 'madman') is connected to it in negated form, just as *bi-'āqilin* (with 'sane') is connected in affirmed form in your saying, 'You are, by the grace of God, sane.' Negation and affirmation are equal in this, just as their equality in your saying, 'Zayd struck 'Amr' and 'Zayd did not strike 'Amr', where you govern the verb in the affirmed and negated forms in one and the same way. Its place is the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), as if he had said: 'You are not a madman, having been favoured by that.' The *bā'* does not prevent *majnūn* from governing what precedes it, because it is extra (*zā'idah*) for emphasizing the negation. The meaning is: a dismissal of what the disbelievers of Makkah attributed to him out of enmity and envy, and that it is part of God's favour upon him, through soundness of intellect and the nobility that befits his qualification for prophethood, in its rank." End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari held, that *bi-ni'mati Rabbika* is connected to *majnūn* and is in the position of a *ḥāl*, requires reflection. When negation applies to a predicate that has a complement, there are two ways of reading it. The first is that the negation applies only to that complement. The second is that the negation applies to the predicate itself, so the complement is negated along with it. To illustrate: when you say, "Zayd is not standing hurriedly" (*mā Zaydun qā'imun musri'an*), the mind immediately takes it that his hurrying is negated but not his standing, so he has stood without hurrying. The other reading is that his standing is negated, and therefore his hurrying is negated too, meaning: there is no standing, so there is no hurrying. The position we have established does not allow al-Zamakhshari's view in any way. Rather, it leads to something that may not be said about the infallible (ﷺ).

It was also said: the meaning is "You are not a madman, and the grace is from your Lord," as in their saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You" (*wa-bi-ḥamdika*), meaning "and the praise is to God." From this is the verse of Labid:

*Wa-ufridtu fi'l-dunyā bi-faqdi 'ashīratī*
*wa-fāraqanī jārun bi-Arbada nāfi'u*

Meaning: "And he (the neighbour) is Arbad." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of *i'rāb* (grammatical analysis).

In *al-Muntakhab* there is a summary of the following: the meaning is that madness was removed from you by the grace of your Lord, that is, the presence of the praiseworthy attribute and the removal of the blameworthy attribute through the bounty of your Lord. Then he established by this claim what amounts to a conclusive proof of its truth, because his blessings were manifest in him: perfect eloquence, intellect, a pleasing conduct, freedom from every defect, and the attainment of every noble quality. So the existence and manifestation of these qualities serves as a certainty that they are lying in their claim that he is mad. "And indeed for you there is a reward that will not end" (*wa-inna laka la-ajran*) is for your bearing their slander and for calling people to God, so what they say shall not stop you from calling to God. "And indeed you are upon a magnificent character" is an explanation of what preceded, "by the grace of your Lord," and a definition for whoever accused him of madness, that he lied and erred, and that one who has such pleasing morals cannot be ascribed madness. The wording indicates superiority and dominance. End of quote.

"And indeed for you there is a reward" means: for what you have borne of the burdens of prophethood, and of their harm, in what they attribute to you, though you are not stained by any of the faults they ascribe. "Not interrupted" (*ghayra mamnūn*) means not cut off. *Mananta al-ḥabl* means "I cut the rope." The poet said:

*Ghubsun kawāsibu lā yumannu ṭa'āmuhā*

meaning: "Grey, predatory birds whose food is not cut off." Mujahid said: "not counted." al-Hasan said: "not tainted by reproach." al-Dahhak said: "without work in return." It was also said: "not measured," which is the meaning of Mujahid's view. al-Zamakhshari said: "Or 'not conferred upon you', because it is a reward you deserve for your deed, and not a gift bestowed at the outset. Only bounties are reproached, not wages for deeds." End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine that human acts and divine justice are rationally determined, associated with the Mu'tazila).

"And indeed you are upon a magnificent character." Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "a magnificent religion; there is no religion more beloved to God than it." 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." 'Ali said: "It is the etiquette of the Qur'an." Qatada said: "It is what he used to enjoin by God's command." It was also said: he was called magnificent because noble qualities were gathered in him: nobility of disposition, purity of nature, a beautiful temperament, and excellence of qualities. Whenever anyone called him, he would say, "Here I am" (*labbayka*). He (ﷺ) said: "God sent me to perfect noble character." He instructed Abu Dharr, saying: "Treat people with good character." From him (ﷺ): "Nothing is placed in the scale heavier than good character." He also said: "The most beloved of you to God are those with the best character."

The apparent connection of *bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn* (which of you is the afflicted one) is to what precedes it. 'Uthman al-Mazini said: "The sentence is complete at His saying '*wa-yubṣirūna*' (and they will see), then he begins with '*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*'." End of quote. Then "*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*" is an interrogative intended to present a choice between two matters. It is known that the judgment is negated of one of them, and the existence (of the truth) specifies it: it is the believer, who is neither afflicted nor has any affliction.

When it is connected to what precedes it, which is the view of the majority, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar said: "The *bā'* is extra, and the meaning is: which of you is the afflicted one?" The *bā'* was added to the subject (mubtada'), as it is added in the phrase *bi-ḥasbika dirhamun*, meaning "your sufficiency is a dirham." al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash said: "The *bā'* is not extra, and *al-maftūn* means 'affliction' (*fitnah*). That is: which of you is it that has the affliction and corruption they called madness?" al-Akhfash also said: "Which of you has been afflicted by affliction?" He omitted the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) and put the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governed noun) in its place. So in his first statement he took *al-maftūn* as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here he kept it as a passive participle and interpreted it by omitting a *muḍāf*. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: "The *bā'* has the meaning of *fī* (in). That is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind?" End of quote. Then the *bā'* is locative, like *Zaydun bi'l-Baṣrah*, meaning "Zayd is in Basra." From this view it appears that the *bā'* in the earlier statement is not locative but causal.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*al-maftūn* means the madman, because he was afflicted (*futina*), that is, tested with madness, or because the Arabs claimed that he was from the delusion of the jinn, and they are the seducers (*al-futtān*) of the seducers among them." End of quote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fī ayyikumu al-maftūn* (in which of you is the afflicted one).

(Sūrat al-Qalam is Makkī, and it has fifty-two verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe.﴾ ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for you is a reward never cut off.﴾ ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ ﴿So you will see and they will see.﴾ ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ [al-Qalam: 7] ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ [al-Qalam: 8] ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise.﴾ [al-Qalam: 9] ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-maker.﴾ [al-Qalam: 10] ﴿A defamer, going about with slander.﴾ [al-Qalam: 11] ﴿A hinderer of good, transgressing and sinful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 12] ﴿Brutal, and after that, of illegitimate birth.﴾ [al-Qalam: 13] ﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Myths of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 15] ﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ [al-Qalam: 16] ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest its fruit at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] ﴿and did not make exception.﴾ [al-Qalam: 18] ﴿So there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep.﴾ [al-Qalam: 19] ﴿And it became like the reaped.﴾ [al-Qalam: 20] ﴿So they called to one another at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 21] ﴿"Go early to your field, if you are going to harvest."﴾ [al-Qalam: 22] ﴿So they set out, while whispering to one another,﴾ [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿"No poor man shall enter it today upon you."﴾ [al-Qalam: 24] ﴿And they went early with determination, as those capable.﴾ [al-Qalam: 25] ﴿But when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ [al-Qalam: 26] ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ [al-Qalam: 27] ﴿Said the most moderate of them, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify Allah?'"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28] ﴿They said, "Exalted is our Lord. Indeed, we have been wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Qalam: 29] ﴿Then they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ [al-Qalam: 30] ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we have been transgressors.﴾ [al-Qalam: 31] ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it. Indeed, we turn to our Lord in desire."﴾ [al-Qalam: 32] ﴿Such is the punishment; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ [al-Qalam: 33] ﴿Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ [al-Qalam: 34] ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35] ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a book in which you study,﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿that indeed for you therein is whatever you choose?﴾ [al-Qalam: 38] ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection, that indeed for you is whatever you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that.﴾ [al-Qalam: 40] ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able.﴾ [al-Qalam: 42] ﴿Their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, while they had been called to prostration when they were sound.﴾ [al-Qalam: 43] ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 45] ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Qalam: 46] ﴿Or is the unseen with them, so they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47] ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief].﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿So his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾ [al-Qalam: 50] ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad!"﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] ﴿But it is not except a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]

(p-305) "al-Mahin" (contemptible): al-Rummani said: the lowly, because of his frequent engagement in ugly deeds, from al-mahana, which is lowness. The root meaning of al-hamz in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: and with his eye and his gesture. An-namim and an-namima are both verbal nouns of (namma), which is conveying what one hears of that which is hurtful and stirs up souls. It was also said: an-namim is the plural of namima, meaning by it the generic noun. Al-'utull: al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the one fierce in contentiousness with falsehood. Ma'mar said: he is the vile and base. The poet said:
"With a brutal man among men, of illegitimate birth, neither courageous nor noble."
It was also said: the one who drags people, i.e., drags them to prison or punishment; and from it: "Seize him and drag him" (khudhuhu fa'tiluhu). Ibn al-Sikkit said: I dragged him ('ataltuhu) and 'atantuhu, with lam and nun. Az-zanim: the pretender (ad-da'iy). Hassan said:
"An illegitimate one, whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the hide's width."
(And he also said):
"You are an illegitimate one, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."
Az-zanim is from az-zamana, which is a piece of goat's skin that is cut off and left hanging from a ring. The pretender was named so because he is an added appendage attached to other than his own people. Wasamahu: he made a mark on him, which is a sign pointing to something. Jarir said:
"When I placed my branding on al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith I slit the nose of al-Akhtal."
Al-Khurtum: the nose; and al-khurtum is one of the attributes of wine. The poet said:
"I have witnessed among them a drinking gathering with a zamir-player, while the people are struck down by a foaming, pale wine."
Ash-Shamantari said: al-khurtum is the first of its flowing out from the jar, and it is also called the nose, for that is its purest and finest. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-khurtum is wine, and he recited for al-A'raj al-Mughanni:
"You spend your day in amusement and play, while at night you are a drinker of the khara'im."
As-Sirram: the gathering of date-palms. Al-Harad: prevention, from their saying: harathat al-ibil, when its milk diminished; and harathat as-sanah, when its rain and goodness diminished, as Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi said; and al-harad is anger. Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim, the companion of al-Asma'i, said: it is lightened (mukhaffaf), and he recited:
"When the steeds come charging, filled with anger and harad."
(And al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said):
"Lions of a thicket met lions unseen, pouring for one another, upon harad, the blood of lions."
Ibn al-Sikkit said: it may be vocalized with a kasra: one says harida, bi'l-kasr, haradan, so he is haradan, and from it it is said: a hared lion, and hawarid lions. Al-harad is also isolation: harada yahridu huruden: he withdrew from his people and descended alone, not mixing with them; and a harud star is one separated from the stars. Al-Asma'i said: al-munharid is the solitary, in the dialect of Hudhayl. End. Al-harad is also intent: harada yahridu, with kasra: he intended; and from it: haradtu hardaka, i.e., I intended your intent. From it is the poet's saying:
"A torrent came from the command of Allah, heading straight as the walled garden."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Bi-ni'mati Rabbika* (by the grace of your Lord) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), as when you say to someone, 'You are, by the praise of God, excellent.'" End of quote. He did not specify what the *bā'* in *bi-ni'mati* is connected to.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*Bi-majnūnin* (with 'madman') is connected to it in negated form, just as *bi-'āqilin* (with 'sane') is connected in affirmed form in your saying, 'You are, by the grace of God, sane.' Negation and affirmation are equal in this, just as their equality in your saying, 'Zayd struck 'Amr' and 'Zayd did not strike 'Amr', where you govern the verb in the affirmed and negated forms in one and the same way. Its place is the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), as if he had said: 'You are not a madman, having been favoured by that.' The *bā'* does not prevent *majnūn* from governing what precedes it, because it is extra (*zā'idah*) for emphasizing the negation. The meaning is: a dismissal of what the disbelievers of Makkah attributed to him out of enmity and envy, and that it is part of God's favour upon him, through soundness of intellect and the nobility that befits his qualification for prophethood, in its rank." End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari held, that *bi-ni'mati Rabbika* is connected to *majnūn* and is in the position of a *ḥāl*, requires reflection. When negation applies to a predicate that has a complement, there are two ways of reading it. The first is that the negation applies only to that complement. The second is that the negation applies to the predicate itself, so the complement is negated along with it. To illustrate: when you say, "Zayd is not standing hurriedly" (*mā Zaydun qā'imun musri'an*), the mind immediately takes it that his hurrying is negated but not his standing, so he has stood without hurrying. The other reading is that his standing is negated, and therefore his hurrying is negated too, meaning: there is no standing, so there is no hurrying. The position we have established does not allow al-Zamakhshari's view in any way. Rather, it leads to something that may not be said about the infallible (ﷺ).

It was also said: the meaning is "You are not a madman, and the grace is from your Lord," as in their saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You" (*wa-bi-ḥamdika*), meaning "and the praise is to God." From this is the verse of Labid:

*Wa-ufridtu fi'l-dunyā bi-faqdi 'ashīratī*
*wa-fāraqanī jārun bi-Arbada nāfi'u*

Meaning: "And he (the neighbour) is Arbad." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of *i'rāb* (grammatical analysis).

In *al-Muntakhab* there is a summary of the following: the meaning is that madness was removed from you by the grace of your Lord, that is, the presence of the praiseworthy attribute and the removal of the blameworthy attribute through the bounty of your Lord. Then he established by this claim what amounts to a conclusive proof of its truth, because his blessings were manifest in him: perfect eloquence, intellect, a pleasing conduct, freedom from every defect, and the attainment of every noble quality. So the existence and manifestation of these qualities serves as a certainty that they are lying in their claim that he is mad. "And indeed for you there is a reward that will not end" (*wa-inna laka la-ajran*) is for your bearing their slander and for calling people to God, so what they say shall not stop you from calling to God. "And indeed you are upon a magnificent character" is an explanation of what preceded, "by the grace of your Lord," and a definition for whoever accused him of madness, that he lied and erred, and that one who has such pleasing morals cannot be ascribed madness. The wording indicates superiority and dominance. End of quote.

"And indeed for you there is a reward" means: for what you have borne of the burdens of prophethood, and of their harm, in what they attribute to you, though you are not stained by any of the faults they ascribe. "Not interrupted" (*ghayra mamnūn*) means not cut off. *Mananta al-ḥabl* means "I cut the rope." The poet said:

*Ghubsun kawāsibu lā yumannu ṭa'āmuhā*

meaning: "Grey, predatory birds whose food is not cut off." Mujahid said: "not counted." al-Hasan said: "not tainted by reproach." al-Dahhak said: "without work in return." It was also said: "not measured," which is the meaning of Mujahid's view. al-Zamakhshari said: "Or 'not conferred upon you', because it is a reward you deserve for your deed, and not a gift bestowed at the outset. Only bounties are reproached, not wages for deeds." End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine that human acts and divine justice are rationally determined, associated with the Mu'tazila).

"And indeed you are upon a magnificent character." Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "a magnificent religion; there is no religion more beloved to God than it." 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." 'Ali said: "It is the etiquette of the Qur'an." Qatada said: "It is what he used to enjoin by God's command." It was also said: he was called magnificent because noble qualities were gathered in him: nobility of disposition, purity of nature, a beautiful temperament, and excellence of qualities. Whenever anyone called him, he would say, "Here I am" (*labbayka*). He (ﷺ) said: "God sent me to perfect noble character." He instructed Abu Dharr, saying: "Treat people with good character." From him (ﷺ): "Nothing is placed in the scale heavier than good character." He also said: "The most beloved of you to God are those with the best character."

The apparent connection of *bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn* (which of you is the afflicted one) is to what precedes it. 'Uthman al-Mazini said: "The sentence is complete at His saying '*wa-yubṣirūna*' (and they will see), then he begins with '*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*'." End of quote. Then "*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*" is an interrogative intended to present a choice between two matters. It is known that the judgment is negated of one of them, and the existence (of the truth) specifies it: it is the believer, who is neither afflicted nor has any affliction.

When it is connected to what precedes it, which is the view of the majority, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar said: "The *bā'* is extra, and the meaning is: which of you is the afflicted one?" The *bā'* was added to the subject (mubtada'), as it is added in the phrase *bi-ḥasbika dirhamun*, meaning "your sufficiency is a dirham." al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash said: "The *bā'* is not extra, and *al-maftūn* means 'affliction' (*fitnah*). That is: which of you is it that has the affliction and corruption they called madness?" al-Akhfash also said: "Which of you has been afflicted by affliction?" He omitted the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) and put the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governed noun) in its place. So in his first statement he took *al-maftūn* as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here he kept it as a passive participle and interpreted it by omitting a *muḍāf*. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: "The *bā'* has the meaning of *fī* (in). That is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind?" End of quote. Then the *bā'* is locative, like *Zaydun bi'l-Baṣrah*, meaning "Zayd is in Basra." From this view it appears that the *bā'* in the earlier statement is not locative but causal.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*al-maftūn* means the madman, because he was afflicted (*futina*), that is, tested with madness, or because the Arabs claimed that he was from the delusion of the jinn, and they are the seducers (*al-futtān*) of the seducers among them." End of quote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fī ayyikumu al-maftūn* (in which of you is the afflicted one).

(Sūrat al-Qalam is Makkī, and it has fifty-two verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe.﴾ ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for you is a reward never cut off.﴾ ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ ﴿So you will see and they will see.﴾ ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ [al-Qalam: 7] ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ [al-Qalam: 8] ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise.﴾ [al-Qalam: 9] ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-maker.﴾ [al-Qalam: 10] ﴿A defamer, going about with slander.﴾ [al-Qalam: 11] ﴿A hinderer of good, transgressing and sinful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 12] ﴿Brutal, and after that, of illegitimate birth.﴾ [al-Qalam: 13] ﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Myths of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 15] ﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ [al-Qalam: 16] ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest its fruit at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] ﴿and did not make exception.﴾ [al-Qalam: 18] ﴿So there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep.﴾ [al-Qalam: 19] ﴿And it became like the reaped.﴾ [al-Qalam: 20] ﴿So they called to one another at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 21] ﴿"Go early to your field, if you are going to harvest."﴾ [al-Qalam: 22] ﴿So they set out, while whispering to one another,﴾ [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿"No poor man shall enter it today upon you."﴾ [al-Qalam: 24] ﴿And they went early with determination, as those capable.﴾ [al-Qalam: 25] ﴿But when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ [al-Qalam: 26] ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ [al-Qalam: 27] ﴿Said the most moderate of them, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify Allah?'"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28] ﴿They said, "Exalted is our Lord. Indeed, we have been wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Qalam: 29] ﴿Then they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ [al-Qalam: 30] ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we have been transgressors.﴾ [al-Qalam: 31] ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it. Indeed, we turn to our Lord in desire."﴾ [al-Qalam: 32] ﴿Such is the punishment; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ [al-Qalam: 33] ﴿Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ [al-Qalam: 34] ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35] ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a book in which you study,﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿that indeed for you therein is whatever you choose?﴾ [al-Qalam: 38] ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection, that indeed for you is whatever you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that.﴾ [al-Qalam: 40] ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able.﴾ [al-Qalam: 42] ﴿Their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, while they had been called to prostration when they were sound.﴾ [al-Qalam: 43] ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 45] ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Qalam: 46] ﴿Or is the unseen with them, so they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47] ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief].﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿So his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾ [al-Qalam: 50] ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad!"﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] ﴿But it is not except a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]

(p-305) "al-Mahin" (contemptible): al-Rummani said: the lowly, because of his frequent engagement in ugly deeds, from al-mahana, which is lowness. The root meaning of al-hamz in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: and with his eye and his gesture. An-namim and an-namima are both verbal nouns of (namma), which is conveying what one hears of that which is hurtful and stirs up souls. It was also said: an-namim is the plural of namima, meaning by it the generic noun. Al-'utull: al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the one fierce in contentiousness with falsehood. Ma'mar said: he is the vile and base. The poet said:
"With a brutal man among men, of illegitimate birth, neither courageous nor noble."
It was also said: the one who drags people, i.e., drags them to prison or punishment; and from it: "Seize him and drag him" (khudhuhu fa'tiluhu). Ibn al-Sikkit said: I dragged him ('ataltuhu) and 'atantuhu, with lam and nun. Az-zanim: the pretender (ad-da'iy). Hassan said:
"An illegitimate one, whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the hide's width."
(And he also said):
"You are an illegitimate one, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."
Az-zanim is from az-zamana, which is a piece of goat's skin that is cut off and left hanging from a ring. The pretender was named so because he is an added appendage attached to other than his own people. Wasamahu: he made a mark on him, which is a sign pointing to something. Jarir said:
"When I placed my branding on al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith I slit the nose of al-Akhtal."
Al-Khurtum: the nose; and al-khurtum is one of the attributes of wine. The poet said:
"I have witnessed among them a drinking gathering with a zamir-player, while the people are struck down by a foaming, pale wine."
Ash-Shamantari said: al-khurtum is the first of its flowing out from the jar, and it is also called the nose, for that is its purest and finest. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-khurtum is wine, and he recited for al-A'raj al-Mughanni:
"You spend your day in amusement and play, while at night you are a drinker of the khara'im."
As-Sirram: the gathering of date-palms. Al-Harad: prevention, from their saying: harathat al-ibil, when its milk diminished; and harathat as-sanah, when its rain and goodness diminished, as Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi said; and al-harad is anger. Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim, the companion of al-Asma'i, said: it is lightened (mukhaffaf), and he recited:
"When the steeds come charging, filled with anger and harad."
(And al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said):
"Lions of a thicket met lions unseen, pouring for one another, upon harad, the blood of lions."
Ibn al-Sikkit said: it may be vocalized with a kasra: one says harida, bi'l-kasr, haradan, so he is haradan, and from it it is said: a hared lion, and hawarid lions. Al-harad is also isolation: harada yahridu huruden: he withdrew from his people and descended alone, not mixing with them; and a harud star is one separated from the stars. Al-Asma'i said: al-munharid is the solitary, in the dialect of Hudhayl. End. Al-harad is also intent: harada yahridu, with kasra: he intended; and from it: haradtu hardaka, i.e., I intended your intent. From it is the poet's saying:
"A torrent came from the command of Allah, heading straight as the walled garden."

(p-306) [Repetition of the verses 1–33 as in the source.]

(p-307) This surah is Makkī. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement about it among any of the people of interpretation. End. Most of it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Abu Jahl. Its connection to what precedes it: in the previous surah He mentioned matters of the state of the blessed and the wretched, and mentioned His overwhelming power and His vast knowledge, and that He, exalted is He, had He willed, would have caused the earth to swallow them or sent upon them a violent wind. What He, exalted is He, informed of was what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received by revelation, while the disbelievers attributed it sometimes to poetry, sometimes to sorcery, and sometimes to madness. So He, glorified and exalted, began this surah by clearing him of what they attributed to him of madness, and by magnifying his reward for his patience upon their harm, and by praising his tremendous character.

(Nūn): a letter of the alphabet, like "Ṣād" and "Qāf", and it is not inflected, like some letters that came with other letters unaffected by governing words. Judging the place of its i'rab is conjecture. What is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it is the name of the great fish upon which the seven earths rest. From Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak: it is the name of the inkwell. From Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, raising it: it is a tablet of light. From Ibn 'Abbas also: it is the last letter of the name al-Rahman. From Ja'far al-Sadiq: it is a river of the rivers of Paradise. Perhaps none of that is sound. Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: "Nūn" is a letter of the alphabet; had it been a complete word it would be inflected as al-qalam is inflected; so it is a letter of spelling, as in all the openings of the surahs. End. Whoever said it is the name of the inkwell or the fish, and claimed it is sworn by like the pen, then if it is a proper noun it should be in the genitive; if feminine it would be non-declined, or if masculine it would be declined; and if it is a common noun it would be inflected and nunated; and none of that applies, so that view is weak. Ibn 'Atiyya said: if it is a name for the inkwell, then either it is a dialect of some Arabs, or an non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized. The poet said:
"When longing for them presses me, the tears of the nun pour forth."
Whoever makes it the Bahamut makes the pen the one that Allah created and commanded to write the creatures, and makes the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to the angels. Whoever says it is a name takes it as the common pen in people's hands. Ibn 'Abbas stated this, and made the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to people, so the oath falls upon this collection: the matter of the Book, which is the foundation of the sciences and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, for the pen is the brother of the tongue and a general blessing from Allah. End. The majority read (Nūn) with a sukūn on the nūn and its idgham into the waw of (wal-qalam) with ghunna, and some people without ghunna; Hamza, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Qalun and Hafs made it clear (izhar). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on the nūn because of the meeting of two sākins. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a fatḥa; this may be a case-ending, and it is a name of the surah sworn by, the preposition is elided so it is in the accusative, not declined due to being a proper noun and feminine, and (wal-qalam) would be conjoined to it. It may also be for the meeting of two sākins, and fatḥa is preferred for lightness, like ayna. (Mā) may be relative or verbal (maṣdariyya). The pronoun in (yasturuna) refers to the scribes, since the pen indicates them; either it means the Recording Angels, or every writer. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by the pen is meant its owners, so the pronoun in (yasturuna) is for them, as if it were said: and the owners of the pen and what they inscribe, or their inscribing. End. This is like His saying: ﴿like darknesses in a deep sea﴾ [al-Nur: 40], meaning "like those of darknesses"; for this reason the pronoun returned to it in His saying: "covered by a wave."

The *bā'* was added to the subject (mubtada'), as it is added in the phrase *bi-ḥasbika dirhamun*, meaning "your sufficiency is a dirham." al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash said: "The *bā'* is not extra, and *al-maftūn* means 'affliction' (*fitnah*). That is: which of you is it that has the affliction and corruption they called madness?" al-Akhfash also said: "Which of you has been afflicted by affliction?" He omitted the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) and put the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governed noun) in its place. So in his first statement he took *al-maftūn* as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here he kept it as a passive participle and interpreted it by omitting a *muḍāf*. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: "The *bā'* has the meaning of *fī* (in). That is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind?" End of quote. Then the *bā'* is locative, like *Zaydun bi'l-Baṣrah*, meaning "Zayd is in Basra." From this view it appears that the *bā'* in the earlier statement is not locative but causal.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*al-maftūn* means the madman, because he was afflicted (*futina*), that is, tested with madness, or because the Arabs claimed that he was from the delusion of the jinn, and they are the seducers (*al-futtān*) of the seducers among them." End of quote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fī ayyikumu al-maftūn* (in which of you is the afflicted one).

(Sūrat al-Qalam is Makkī, and it has fifty-two verses.)
(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.)
﴿Nūn. By the pen and what they inscribe.﴾ ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ ﴿Indeed, for you is a reward never cut off.﴾ ﴿And indeed, you are of a tremendous character.﴾ ﴿So you will see and they will see.﴾ ﴿Which of you is the afflicted one.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ [al-Qalam: 7] ﴿So do not obey the deniers.﴾ [al-Qalam: 8] ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise.﴾ [al-Qalam: 9] ﴿And do not obey every contemptible oath-maker.﴾ [al-Qalam: 10] ﴿A defamer, going about with slander.﴾ [al-Qalam: 11] ﴿A hinderer of good, transgressing and sinful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 12] ﴿Brutal, and after that, of illegitimate birth.﴾ [al-Qalam: 13] ﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ [al-Qalam: 14] ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Myths of the ancients."﴾ [al-Qalam: 15] ﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ [al-Qalam: 16] ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore to harvest its fruit at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 17] ﴿and did not make exception.﴾ [al-Qalam: 18] ﴿So there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep.﴾ [al-Qalam: 19] ﴿And it became like the reaped.﴾ [al-Qalam: 20] ﴿So they called to one another at morning,﴾ [al-Qalam: 21] ﴿"Go early to your field, if you are going to harvest."﴾ [al-Qalam: 22] ﴿So they set out, while whispering to one another,﴾ [al-Qalam: 23] ﴿"No poor man shall enter it today upon you."﴾ [al-Qalam: 24] ﴿And they went early with determination, as those capable.﴾ [al-Qalam: 25] ﴿But when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ [al-Qalam: 26] ﴿Rather, we are deprived.﴾ [al-Qalam: 27] ﴿Said the most moderate of them, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify Allah?'"﴾ [al-Qalam: 28] ﴿They said, "Exalted is our Lord. Indeed, we have been wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Qalam: 29] ﴿Then they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ [al-Qalam: 30] ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we have been transgressors.﴾ [al-Qalam: 31] ﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it. Indeed, we turn to our Lord in desire."﴾ [al-Qalam: 32] ﴿Such is the punishment; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew.﴾ [al-Qalam: 33] ﴿Indeed, for the righteous with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ [al-Qalam: 34] ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ [al-Qalam: 35] ﴿What is wrong with you? How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a book in which you study,﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿that indeed for you therein is whatever you choose?﴾ [al-Qalam: 38] ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection, that indeed for you is whatever you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that.﴾ [al-Qalam: 40] ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able.﴾ [al-Qalam: 42] ﴿Their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, while they had been called to prostration when they were sound.﴾ [al-Qalam: 43] ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 45] ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Qalam: 46] ﴿Or is the unseen with them, so they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47] ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief].﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿So his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾ [al-Qalam: 50] ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad!"﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] ﴿But it is not except a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]

(p-305) "al-Mahin" (contemptible): al-Rummani said: the lowly, because of his frequent engagement in ugly deeds, from al-mahana, which is lowness. The root meaning of al-hamz in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: and with his eye and his gesture. An-namim and an-namima are both verbal nouns of (namma), which is conveying what one hears of that which is hurtful and stirs up souls. It was also said: an-namim is the plural of namima, meaning by it the generic noun. Al-'utull: al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the one fierce in contentiousness with falsehood. Ma'mar said: he is the vile and base. The poet said:
"With a brutal man among men, of illegitimate birth, neither courageous nor noble."
It was also said: the one who drags people, i.e., drags them to prison or punishment; and from it: "Seize him and drag him" (khudhuhu fa'tiluhu). Ibn al-Sikkit said: I dragged him ('ataltuhu) and 'atantuhu, with lam and nun. Az-zanim: the pretender (ad-da'iy). Hassan said:
"An illegitimate one, whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the hide's width."
(And he also said):
"You are an illegitimate one, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."
Az-zanim is from az-zamana, which is a piece of goat's skin that is cut off and left hanging from a ring. The pretender was named so because he is an added appendage attached to other than his own people. Wasamahu: he made a mark on him, which is a sign pointing to something. Jarir said:
"When I placed my branding on al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith I slit the nose of al-Akhtal."
Al-Khurtum: the nose; and al-khurtum is one of the attributes of wine. The poet said:
"I have witnessed among them a drinking gathering with a zamir-player, while the people are struck down by a foaming, pale wine."
Ash-Shamantari said: al-khurtum is the first of its flowing out from the jar, and it is also called the nose, for that is its purest and finest. An-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-khurtum is wine, and he recited for al-A'raj al-Mughanni:
"You spend your day in amusement and play, while at night you are a drinker of the khara'im."
As-Sirram: the gathering of date-palms. Al-Harad: prevention, from their saying: harathat al-ibil, when its milk diminished; and harathat as-sanah, when its rain and goodness diminished, as Abu 'Ubayd and al-Qutabi said; and al-harad is anger. Abu Nasr Ahmad ibn Hatim, the companion of al-Asma'i, said: it is lightened (mukhaffaf), and he recited:
"When the steeds come charging, filled with anger and harad."
(And al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said):
"Lions of a thicket met lions unseen, pouring for one another, upon harad, the blood of lions."
Ibn al-Sikkit said: it may be vocalized with a kasra: one says harida, bi'l-kasr, haradan, so he is haradan, and from it it is said: a hared lion, and hawarid lions. Al-harad is also isolation: harada yahridu huruden: he withdrew from his people and descended alone, not mixing with them; and a harud star is one separated from the stars. Al-Asma'i said: al-munharid is the solitary, in the dialect of Hudhayl. End. Al-harad is also intent: harada yahridu, with kasra: he intended; and from it: haradtu hardaka, i.e., I intended your intent. From it is the poet's saying:
"A torrent came from the command of Allah, heading straight as the walled garden."

(p-306) [Repetition of the verses 1–33 as in the source.]

(p-307) This surah is Makkī. Ibn 'Atiyya said: there is no disagreement about it among any of the people of interpretation. End. Most of it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and Abu Jahl. Its connection to what precedes it: in the previous surah He mentioned matters of the state of the blessed and the wretched, and mentioned His overwhelming power and His vast knowledge, and that He, exalted is He, had He willed, would have caused the earth to swallow them or sent upon them a violent wind. What He, exalted is He, informed of was what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received by revelation, while the disbelievers attributed it sometimes to poetry, sometimes to sorcery, and sometimes to madness. So He, glorified and exalted, began this surah by clearing him of what they attributed to him of madness, and by magnifying his reward for his patience upon their harm, and by praising his tremendous character.

(Nūn): a letter of the alphabet, like "Ṣād" and "Qāf", and it is not inflected, like some letters that came with other letters unaffected by governing words. Judging the place of its i'rab is conjecture. What is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid: it is the name of the great fish upon which the seven earths rest. From Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak: it is the name of the inkwell. From Mu'awiya ibn Qurra, raising it: it is a tablet of light. From Ibn 'Abbas also: it is the last letter of the name al-Rahman. From Ja'far al-Sadiq: it is a river of the rivers of Paradise. Perhaps none of that is sound. Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qushayri said in his tafsir: "Nūn" is a letter of the alphabet; had it been a complete word it would be inflected as al-qalam is inflected; so it is a letter of spelling, as in all the openings of the surahs. End. Whoever said it is the name of the inkwell or the fish, and claimed it is sworn by like the pen, then if it is a proper noun it should be in the genitive; if feminine it would be non-declined, or if masculine it would be declined; and if it is a common noun it would be inflected and nunated; and none of that applies, so that view is weak. Ibn 'Atiyya said: if it is a name for the inkwell, then either it is a dialect of some Arabs, or an non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized. The poet said:
"When longing for them presses me, the tears of the nun pour forth."
Whoever makes it the Bahamut makes the pen the one that Allah created and commanded to write the creatures, and makes the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to the angels. Whoever says it is a name takes it as the common pen in people's hands. Ibn 'Abbas stated this, and made the pronoun in (yasturuna) refer to people, so the oath falls upon this collection: the matter of the Book, which is the foundation of the sciences and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, for the pen is the brother of the tongue and a general blessing from Allah. End. The majority read (Nūn) with a sukūn on the nūn and its idgham into the waw of (wal-qalam) with ghunna, and some people without ghunna; Hamza, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Qalun and Hafs made it clear (izhar). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on the nūn because of the meeting of two sākins. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Isa, with a variant from him, read it with a fatḥa; this may be a case-ending, and it is a name of the surah sworn by, the preposition is elided so it is in the accusative, not declined due to being a proper noun and feminine, and (wal-qalam) would be conjoined to it. It may also be for the meeting of two sākins, and fatḥa is preferred for lightness, like ayna. (Mā) may be relative or verbal (maṣdariyya). The pronoun in (yasturuna) refers to the scribes, since the pen indicates them; either it means the Recording Angels, or every writer. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that by the pen is meant its owners, so the pronoun in (yasturuna) is for them, as if it were said: and the owners of the pen and what they inscribe, or their inscribing. End. This is like His saying: ﴿like darknesses in a deep sea﴾ [al-Nur: 40], meaning "like those of darknesses"; for this reason the pronoun returned to it in His saying: "covered by a wave."

The answer to the oath is: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ It appears that "by the grace of your Lord" is an oath inserted as a parenthesis between the subject and the predicate, for emphasis, to strengthen the assertion, and to stress the complete negation of the blameworthy attribute from him (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "*Bi-ni'mati Rabbika* (by the grace of your Lord) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ), as when you say to someone, 'You are, by the praise of God, excellent.'" End of quote. He did not specify what the *bā'* in *bi-ni'mati* is connected to.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*Bi-majnūnin* (with 'madman') is connected to it in negated form, just as *bi-'āqilin* (with 'sane') is connected in affirmed form in your saying, 'You are, by the grace of God, sane.' Negation and affirmation are equal in this, just as their equality in your saying, 'Zayd struck 'Amr' and 'Zayd did not strike 'Amr', where you govern the verb in the affirmed and negated forms in one and the same way. Its place is the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), as if he had said: 'You are not a madman, having been favoured by that.' The *bā'* does not prevent *majnūn* from governing what precedes it, because it is extra (*zā'idah*) for emphasizing the negation. The meaning is: a dismissal of what the disbelievers of Makkah attributed to him out of enmity and envy, and that it is part of God's favour upon him, through soundness of intellect and the nobility that befits his qualification for prophethood, in its rank." End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari held, that *bi-ni'mati Rabbika* is connected to *majnūn* and is in the position of a *ḥāl*, requires reflection. When negation applies to a predicate that has a complement, there are two ways of reading it. The first is that the negation applies only to that complement. The second is that the negation applies to the predicate itself, so the complement is negated along with it. To illustrate: when you say, "Zayd is not standing hurriedly" (*mā Zaydun qā'imun musri'an*), the mind immediately takes it that his hurrying is negated but not his standing, so he has stood without hurrying. The other reading is that his standing is negated, and therefore his hurrying is negated too, meaning: there is no standing, so there is no hurrying. The position we have established does not allow al-Zamakhshari's view in any way. Rather, it leads to something that may not be said about the infallible (ﷺ).

It was also said: the meaning is "You are not a madman, and the grace is from your Lord," as in their saying, "Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You" (*wa-bi-ḥamdika*), meaning "and the praise is to God." From this is the verse of Labid:

*Wa-ufridtu fi'l-dunyā bi-faqdi 'ashīratī*
*wa-fāraqanī jārun bi-Arbada nāfi'u*

Meaning: "And he (the neighbour) is Arbad." End of quote. This is an explanation of meaning, not an explanation of *i'rāb* (grammatical analysis).

In *al-Muntakhab* there is a summary of the following: the meaning is that madness was removed from you by the grace of your Lord, that is, the presence of the praiseworthy attribute and the removal of the blameworthy attribute through the bounty of your Lord. Then he established by this claim what amounts to a conclusive proof of its truth, because his blessings were manifest in him: perfect eloquence, intellect, a pleasing conduct, freedom from every defect, and the attainment of every noble quality. So the existence and manifestation of these qualities serves as a certainty that they are lying in their claim that he is mad. "And indeed for you there is a reward that will not end" (*wa-inna laka la-ajran*) is for your bearing their slander and for calling people to God, so what they say shall not stop you from calling to God. "And indeed you are upon a magnificent character" is an explanation of what preceded, "by the grace of your Lord," and a definition for whoever accused him of madness, that he lied and erred, and that one who has such pleasing morals cannot be ascribed madness. The wording indicates superiority and dominance. End of quote.

"And indeed for you there is a reward" means: for what you have borne of the burdens of prophethood, and of their harm, in what they attribute to you, though you are not stained by any of the faults they ascribe. "Not interrupted" (*ghayra mamnūn*) means not cut off. *Mananta al-ḥabl* means "I cut the rope." The poet said:

*Ghubsun kawāsibu lā yumannu ṭa'āmuhā*

meaning: "Grey, predatory birds whose food is not cut off." Mujahid said: "not counted." al-Hasan said: "not tainted by reproach." al-Dahhak said: "without work in return." It was also said: "not measured," which is the meaning of Mujahid's view. al-Zamakhshari said: "Or 'not conferred upon you', because it is a reward you deserve for your deed, and not a gift bestowed at the outset. Only bounties are reproached, not wages for deeds." End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilism (the doctrine that human acts and divine justice are rationally determined, associated with the Mu'tazila).

"And indeed you are upon a magnificent character." Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: "a magnificent religion; there is no religion more beloved to God than it." 'A'isha said: "His character was the Qur'an." 'Ali said: "It is the etiquette of the Qur'an." Qatada said: "It is what he used to enjoin by God's command." It was also said: he was called magnificent because noble qualities were gathered in him: nobility of disposition, purity of nature, a beautiful temperament, and excellence of qualities. Whenever anyone called him, he would say, "Here I am" (*labbayka*). He (ﷺ) said: "God sent me to perfect noble character." He instructed Abu Dharr, saying: "Treat people with good character." From him (ﷺ): "Nothing is placed in the scale heavier than good character." He also said: "The most beloved of you to God are those with the best character."

The apparent connection of *bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn* (which of you is the afflicted one) is to what precedes it. 'Uthman al-Mazini said: "The sentence is complete at His saying '*wa-yubṣirūna*' (and they will see), then he begins with '*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*'." End of quote. Then "*bi-ayyikumu al-maftūn*" is an interrogative intended to present a choice between two matters. It is known that the judgment is negated of one of them, and the existence (of the truth) specifies it: it is the believer, who is neither afflicted nor has any affliction.

When it is connected to what precedes it, which is the view of the majority, Qatada and Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar said: "The *bā'* is extra, and the meaning is: which of you is the afflicted one?" The *bā'* was added to the subject (mubtada'), as it is added in the phrase *bi-ḥasbika dirhamun*, meaning "your sufficiency is a dirham." al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and al-Akhfash said: "The *bā'* is not extra, and *al-maftūn* means 'affliction' (*fitnah*). That is: which of you is it that has the affliction and corruption they called madness?" al-Akhfash also said: "Which of you has been afflicted by affliction?" He omitted the *muḍāf* (the governing noun) and put the *muḍāf ilayhi* (the governed noun) in its place. So in his first statement he took *al-maftūn* as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here he kept it as a passive participle and interpreted it by omitting a *muḍāf*. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: "The *bā'* has the meaning of *fī* (in). That is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind?" End of quote. Then the *bā'* is locative, like *Zaydun bi'l-Baṣrah*, meaning "Zayd is in Basra." From this view it appears that the *bā'* in the earlier statement is not locative but causal.

al-Zamakhshari said: "*al-maftūn* means the madman, because he was afflicted (*futina*), that is, tested with madness, or because the Arabs claimed that he was from the delusion of the jinn, and they are the seducers (*al-futtān*) of the seducers among them." End of quote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read: *fī ayyikumu al-maftūn* (in which of you is the afflicted one).

How do you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 36] ﴿Or do you have a book in which you study,﴾ [al-Qalam: 37] ﴿that indeed for you therein is whatever you choose?﴾ [al-Qalam: 38] ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, extending to the Day of Resurrection, that indeed for you is whatever you judge?﴾ [al-Qalam: 39] ﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that.﴾ [al-Qalam: 40] ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ [al-Qalam: 41] ﴿On the Day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able.﴾ [al-Qalam: 42] ﴿Their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, while they had been called to prostration when they were sound.﴾ [al-Qalam: 43] ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse. We will lead them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] ﴿And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [al-Qalam: 45] ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment, so they are burdened with debt?﴾ [al-Qalam: 46] ﴿Or is the unseen with them, so they write it down?﴾ [al-Qalam: 47] ﴿So be patient for the decree of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish, when he called out while he was suppressing [his grief].﴾ [al-Qalam: 48] ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord overtaken him, he would have been cast out onto the open wasteland while he was blameworthy.﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿So his Lord chose him and made him among the righteous.﴾ [al-Qalam: 50] ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is mad!"﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] ﴿But it is not except a reminder to the worlds.﴾ [al-Qalam: 52]

(p-305) "al-Mahin" (contemptible): al-Rummani said: the lowly, because of his frequent engagement in ugly deeds, from al-mahana, which is lowness. The root meaning of al-hamz in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: and with his eye and his gesture. An-namim and an-namima are both verbal nouns of (namma), which is conveying what one hears of that which is hurtful and stirs up souls. It was also said: an-namim is the plural of namima, meaning by it the generic noun. Al-'utull: al-Kalbi and al-Farra' said: the one fierce in contentiousness with falsehood. Ma'mar said: he is the vile and base. The poet said:
"With a brutal man among men, of illegitimate birth, neither courageous nor noble."
It was also said: the one who drags people, i.e., drags them to prison or punishment; and from it: "Seize him and drag him" (khudhuhu fa'tiluhu). Ibn al-Sikkit said: I dragged him ('ataltuhu) and 'atantuhu, with lam and nun. Az-zanim: the pretender (ad-da'iy). Hassan said:
"An illegitimate one, whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the hide's width."
(And he also said):
"You are an illegitimate one, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."
Az-zanim is from az-zamana, which is a piece of goat's skin that is cut off and left hanging from a ring. The pretender was named so because he is an added appendage attached to other than his own people. Wasamahu: he made a mark on him, which is a sign pointing to something. Jarir said:
"When I placed my branding on al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith I slit the nose of al-Akhtal."
