But what is in my memory is that it is transitive with "ala," as in the words of the poet:

I went out to him early in the morning and saw him
sitting upon him in al-Sarim, his blamers around him.

"In kuntum sarimin": the apparent meaning is that it is from the harvesting of palm trees. It was said: it may also mean: if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion, from your saying "a sharp sword" (sayf sarim).

"Yatakhafatun" (they whisper): they conceal their speech out of fear that the needy might perceive them. "An la yadkhulannaha" means: they whispered this statement, "No needy person shall enter it today." "An" is a verbal particle, and it may also be an explanatory particle. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "la yadkhulanna" without "an," either with the implied "yaqulun" (they say), or by treating "yatakhafatun" as equivalent to speech, since its meaning is "they speak secretly." The prohibition against entering is a prohibition against enabling it, meaning: do not enable them to enter, lest they enter.

"Wa ghadaw 'ala harding qadirin": that is, with intention and capability within themselves, thinking they had attained their goal. Ibn 'Abbas said this, meaning: heading to their garden swiftly, considering themselves capable of harvesting it. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: "'ala harding" means "upon prevention," meaning: capable within themselves of preventing the needy from its good. So God repaid them by preventing them from good. Al-Hasan said: "'ala harding" means in need and poverty. Al-Sudi and Sufyan said: "'ala harding" means in anger, meaning they were capable only of rage and anger toward one another. It was also said: "'ala harding" means "in isolation," meaning they went out alone without the needy. Al-Azhari said: "harding" is the name of their village. Al-Sudi said: it is the name of their garden, meaning they went out to that garden capable of harvesting it in their own estimation, or determining that their goal of harvesting would be accomplished for them. It was said that it may mean "taqdir" in the sense of constriction, based on God's words: ﴿and whoever has his provision restricted﴾ (65:7), meaning: constricting the needy, since they withheld from them what their father used to give them from it.

"Fa-lamma ra'awha": that is, in the condition in which they had set out upon it, from its destruction and the departure of its good, they said: "Indeed we have gone astray," meaning: we have lost the way to it. Qatada said this. At first they denied that it was it, and believed they had taken a wrong path to it; then it became clear to them that it was it, and that a punishment from God had befallen it that took away its good. It was also said: "Indeed we have gone astray" from the right course in our going out with the intention of preventing the needy. So they said: "Rather, we are deprived of its good through our betrayal of ourselves."

The most moderate of them said, meaning the best and most sound in judgment: "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify (God)?'" ﴿Why do you not glorify [God]?﴾ (68:28). He reprimanded and rebuked them for abandoning what he had urged upon them of glorifying God, that is, remembering Him and declaring Him free of imperfection. Had they remembered God and His kindness toward them, they would have complied with what He commanded of sharing with the needy and followed their father's practice in that. When they neglected the remembrance of God (exalted is He) and resolved to withhold from the needy, God tested them. This indicates that the most moderate of them had previously come to them and urged them to remember God (exalted is He). Mujahid and Abu Salih said: their exception was "Glory be to God." Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid made the glorification (tasbih) a substitute for "if God wills," because the meaning is declaring God free from anything occurring except by His will. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are united in the sense of glorifying God, since the exception is a committing of the matter to Him, and glorification is declaring Him free of imperfection, and each of committing and declaring free is an exaltation of Him. It was also said: "lawla tusabbihun" means "lawla tastaghfirun" (why do you not seek forgiveness?).

When he reprimanded them, they returned to the remembrance of God (exalted is He), acknowledged against themselves their wrongdoing, and hastened to glorify God (exalted is He), saying: "Glory be to our Lord." Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, we seek God's forgiveness for our sin. When they confessed their wrongdoing, some of them blamed others, and placed the blame on other than themselves, since among them there was one who adorned the plan, one who accepted it, one who ordered restraint, one who disobeyed the order, and one who remained silent with consent. Then they acknowledged that they had transgressed, and hoped, awaiting relief, that their Lord would give them in exchange something better than that garden: "Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it," meaning: in exchange for this garden, something better than it. The discussion of this has preceded in (the commentary on) al-Kahf, and the disagreement over the light and heavy pronunciation of "yubaddilana," as attributed to the readers, is known.

﴿Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire﴾ (68:32), meaning: we seek to receive good from Him. The apparent view is that the People of this garden were believers who committed a sin and repented. It was also said: they were from the People of the Book. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "It has reached me that the people called upon God and were sincere, and God knew from them the truth, so He gave them in exchange a garden, and every cluster of it was like a black-skinned man standing." From Mujahid: they repented, so they were given in exchange something better than it. Al-Qushayri said: most of them say that they repented and were sincere. End of quote. Al-Hasan hesitated about whether they were believers, and said: "Was their saying, 'Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire,' a (genuine) faith, or was it in the manner of the polytheists when hardship afflicts them?"

﴿Such is the punishment﴾ (68:33). This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the affair of Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reference by "such" is to the punishment that descended upon the Garden, that is, such is the punishment (that is), the one that descended upon Quraysh suddenly; then the punishment of the Hereafter after that is more severe for them than the punishment of this world. Many of the exegetes said: the punishment descended upon Quraysh, paralleling the affair of the Garden, is the drought that befell them for seven years, until they saw smoke and ate hides. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: like that punishment with which We tested the people of Mecca and the People of the Garden is the punishment of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and greater than it. End of quote.

The comparison of the trial of Quraysh with the trial of the People of the Garden is that the People of the Garden resolved to benefit from its fruit and deprive the needy, so God (exalted is He) turned it against them and deprived them. And when Quraysh went out to Badr, they swore to kill the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions; when they did that, they would return to Mecca, circle the Ka'ba, and drink wine, so God turned it against them by having them killed and captured. When He punished them with that in this world, He said: "And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 68, verse 7–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best﴾ is a warning to the astray, and they are, in reality, the madmen, since they had intellects which they did not benefit from and did not use for what the Messengers brought. Or ("knows best") may be a metaphor for the recompense of both groups. ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾, i.e., those who denied what Allah revealed to you of the Revelation. This is a prohibition against obeying them in anything of what they called him to, such as glorifying their gods. ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾: "law" (lau) here, according to the opinion of the Basrans, is a verbal particle with the meaning of "an" (that), i.e., they wish for your compromise. The discussion of this was mentioned in His – exalted is He – saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾. The view of the majority is that the object of "wadda" (wish) is omitted, i.e., they wish for your compromise, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, and "law" remains in its original sense as a conditional particle, meaning that what would have occurred did not occur because something else did not occur, and its answer is omitted, its estimated meaning being: they would have been pleased by that.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, ʿAtiyya and al-Suddi said: "law tudhin" means "law takfur" (if you were to disbelieve), so that they persist in their disbelief. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas as well: "if you were to be lenient with them, so they would be lenient with you." Qatada said: "if you were to turn away from this matter, so they would turn away with you." Al-Hasan said: "if you were to flatter them in your religion, so they would flatter you in their religion." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "if you were to be hypocritical and ostentatious, so they would be hypocritical with you and show off to you." Al-Rabi ibn Anas said: "if you were to lie, so they would lie." Abu Jaʿfar said: "if you were to weaken, so they would weaken." Al-Kalbi and al-Farra said: "if you were to soften, so they would soften." Aban ibn Thaʿlab said: "if you were to show favouritism, so they would be favoured." And they said other than these sayings.

Al-Farra said: "al-dihan" means softening (talyin). Al-Mufaddal said: hypocrisy and abandoning sincere advice. This is the transmission of the lexicographers, and what they said does not go beyond this, because what differs from this is an explanation by a necessary consequence. ﴿So they would compromise﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you would compromise﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He diverted it to another way, which is that it is made the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then they compromise", like His saying: ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord fears not﴾, meaning: they wish that you would compromise, so they then compromise, or they wish for your compromise, so they now compromise in hope of your compromise. End.

The majority of the codices have the nun. Harun said: in some codices it is ﴿fa-yudhinu﴾ (so that they compromise) with a naṣb (accusative), and for its accusative there are two possibilities: one is that it is the answer to "wadda" because it includes the meaning of "layta" (would that), and the second is that it is in the assumption that it was pronounced with "an", i.e., they wish that you would compromise so that they would compromise, so it is a coordination with the assumption. This second possibility does not arise except according to the view of the one who makes "law" a verbal particle with the meaning of "an".

﴿Do not obey every oath-taker, contemptible﴾. The explanation of "mahin" and what follows it was given earlier in the vocabulary (al-mufradat), and these attributes came as intensive forms (ṣifat mubalagha). The rhyme was observed in them, so ﴿ḥallaf﴾ (oath-taker) is followed by ﴿mahin﴾ (contemptible), because the nun in them with the mim is a kind of correspondence. Then came: ﴿hammaz, mashsha' bi-namim﴾ (a slanderer, going about with gossip), with the two intensive attributes (p-310). Then came: ﴿mannaʿ lil-khayr muʿtad athim﴾ (withholding from good, transgressing, sinful). So mannaʿ and athim are intensive attributes. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" (good) here is meant in its general sense, in whatever is called good. It was said: "khayr" here means wealth; he means one who withholds wealth, expressing by it stinginess. Its meaning: one who exceeds the limit in wrongdoing.

In the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, I said — meaning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — "What is the ʿutull, the zanim?" He said: "The one of wide belly, the one of ill-natured creation, the one who eats much and drinks much, the one who is cruel and wrongdoing." Al-Hasan read ʿutullin with a raised lam (ʿutullun), while the majority read it with a lowered lam after that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made his harshness and his arrogance his worst faults, because when he is harsh and his nature is coarse, his heart becomes hard, and he becomes bold toward every disobedience. Also, because it is generally the case that when a drop of semen is corrupt, the offspring from it becomes corrupt. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his child, nor his grandchild." And "after that" is in the sense of "then" in His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾. Al-Hasan read ʿutullun in the nominative, as a dispraise, and this reading strengthens what is indicated after that. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "after that" means: after we described him with it. So this order is only in the speech of the describer, not in the occurrence of those attributes in the one described; otherwise, his being ʿutull is prior to his being one who has wealth and withholds it. End.

"Zanim" means one who is attached to a people while not being from them, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others. It was also said: the zanim is the suspect, the one of ugly deeds. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the zanim is one who has a zanama (a growth) on his neck like the zanama of a sheep, and we did not know the one referred to until it was revealed, and we recognised him by his zanama. End.

It is reported that al-Akhnas ibn Sharif had this attribute; he had a zanama. Ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the zanim is the one known for evil, just as a sheep is known by its zanama. And also from him: that he is the one known for ignoble lineage. And also from him: that he is the wrongdoer. From ʿIkrima: he is the base. From Mujahid, ʿIkrima and Ibn al-Musayyab: that he is the child of fornication attached in lineage to the people. Al-Walid was a claimed son among Quraysh, not of their stock; his father claimed him eighteen years after his birth. Mujahid said: he had six fingers on his hand, with an extra finger on each thumb.

What appears is that these attributes are not specific to one individual. Do you not see His saying: ﴿every oath-taker﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed We have tested them﴾? The prohibition was only against obeying one who has these attributes.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said, summarized: The two Nahwis, the two Harams, Hafs and the people of Madina read ﴿an kana﴾ as a statement; the rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Jaʿfar read it as a question. Hamza made both hamzas clear, and the rest eased the second. As for the statement reading, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that ʿutull act upon it, even though it has been described. End. This is the view of the Kufans, and it is not permissible according to the Basrans. It was also said: "zanim" (in the sense of "an kana" with "zanim") especially according to the view of the one who interpreted it as "ill-natured in deeds."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying "do not obey", i.e., do not obey him with these faults, because he has wealth, i.e., because of his affluence and his share of this world. It is also permissible that it is connected to what follows it, in the sense of: because he is one who has wealth and is supported by sons, ﴿he denies Our signs﴾, and it does not act upon it. The one who is the answer of "idha" (when)… because what follows the condition does not act upon what precedes it, but what the sentence indicates of the meaning of denial. End.

As for the interrogative reading, it is possible that a verb is supplied which is indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he be obeyed because he has wealth?" Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "would you obey him because he has wealth?" Or a verb indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he deny or deny outright because he has wealth?"

Nafi, in the narration of al-Yazidi from him, read ﴿in kana﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: the condition is addressed to the addressee, i.e., do not obey every oath-taker making his affluence a condition; because when he obeys the disbeliever for his wealth, it is as if he made affluence a condition of obedience. Directing the condition to the addressee is like directing the hope to him in His saying: ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾. End.

And the sayings: "an kana" is a condition, and "idha tutla" is a condition; so this is a case where two conditions are combined, and they are not among the conditions whose occurrence is ordered. The one that comes later in wording is the one that comes first, and the one that comes first in wording is a condition for the second, as in his verse:

"If I stumble after this, if my soul is drawn from here, then say: no, no."

Because what prevents attention to the signs of Allah is his having wealth and sons; he is preoccupied in heart, so he is heedless of reflection and thought. The world has taken hold of him and made him insolent.

Al-Hasan read ﴿a-idha﴾ as an interrogative, and it is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach for his saying: "The Qur'an is the fables of the ancients", when the signs of Allah were recited to him. When he mentioned his evil deeds and sayings, he mentioned what will be done to him by way of threat, saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. The branding is the mark.

Since the face is the noblest part of man, and the nose is the most honoured of the face because it is foremost, for this reason they made it the place of might and zeal, and derived from it the word "anafa" (pride), and they said: "one with zealous nose, lofty of the bridge"; and of the humiliated they said: "his nose was cut off" and "his nose was rubbed in the dust." It was also a place where marks appear for elevation. He said: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾, and this is the utmost of humiliation, contempt and enslavement, since he became like a beast which cannot repel its branding on the nose. If branding on the face is a disfigurement, how much more so on the most honoured limb of it? It has been said: beauty is in the nose; and some men of letters said:

"The beauty of a young man is in the nose, and the nose is bare, so how is it when the mole becomes an ornament for it?"

﴿We shall brand him﴾ is a future verb whose time is not fixed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is striking with the sword, i.e., he is struck on his face and on his nose, so that will be like branding on the nose, and that happened to him on the day of Badr. Al-Mubarrad said: that is in the punishment of the Hereafter, in Jahannam, and it is torment by fire on their noses. Others said: that is on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., we shall brand his nose with a mark by which his disbelief and the lowering of his rank will be recognised. Qatada and others said: its meaning is that We shall do to him in this world of blame, hatred and notoriety for evil what will remain on him and not be hidden, so that will be like a branding on the nose, firm and clear, as you say: "I shall put a collar on you like the collar of the dove", meaning: I shall make the matter clear in you. In this sense Jarir meant by his saying:

"When I placed my branding-iron upon al-Farazdaq"

In branding on the nose there is disfigurement, so its metaphorical use for dispraised things came highly eloquent. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: If you consider the state of Abu Jahl and his like, and what was established for them in this world of evil consequences in the Hereafter, you will see that they were branded on the snouts. End. Abu al-ʿAliya and Muqatil, and al-Farra preferred it, said: his face will blacken before entering the Fire, and He mentioned the snout, while the intended meaning is the face, because part of the face stands for part of it. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: The disbeliever only went to extremes in enmity to the Messenger (ﷺ) because of pride and zeal; so, since the witness of rejection is pride and zeal, He expressed this specificity by His saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. End of his words. In using "khurtum" (snout) in place of "anf" (nose) there is contempt and disdain, because the true meaning of "khurtum" belongs to beasts of prey.

It is concluded from this whether His saying "We shall brand him upon the snout" is literal or metaphorical; and if it is literal, is that in this world or in the Hereafter? Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, in his tafsir, went far in interpreting "khurtum" as wine, meaning: We shall flog him for drinking it.

When he described those who possess these blameworthy qualities, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh, He (exalted is He) informed them of what befell them of trial through drought and hunger, in response to the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Joseph," the hadith in full. (This was) like how We tested the People of the Garden, whose story was known to them. It was a garden in the land of Yemen, at San'a, belonging to a man who used to pay God's due from it. When he died it passed to his son, and they withheld its bounty from the people and were stingy with God's due, so God (exalted is He) destroyed it from a direction they could not repel what had befallen them. It was also said: it was at Suran, a few farsakhs from San'a, belonging to a people after the raising of Jesus (peace be upon him). Its owner used to give to the needy what the sickle missed, what lay at the bottom of the heaps, what the grape-picking missed, and what remained on the palm-fronds under the palm tree when it was harvested. A great deal would gather for them. When he died his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will become constrained for us, and we have dependents." So they swore that they would harvest it at dawn in the darkness, secretly from the needy, and they did not make an exception in their oath.

The kaf in "kama" (as) is in the accusative position, and "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. It was also said: "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and "idh" is the object of "balawnahum" (We tested them). "Layasrimunnaha" is the answer to the oath, not a quotation of their own words, for had it been their words it would have been "lanasrimanna" with the first-person plural. The meaning: they would certainly gather its fruit when they entered in the morning, before the needy came out in their usual habit with their father. "Wa la yastathnun" means: they did not turn back from what they had resolved upon of denying the needy. Mujahid said: its meaning is that they did not say "if God wills," but resolved upon that with the resolve of one who controls his own affair. Al-Zamakhshari, following Mujahid's view, said: "nor did they say, 'if God wills.'" (If you ask) why is it called an exception (istithna') when it is only a condition (shart)? (I answer): because it performs the function of an exception, since the meaning of your saying, "I will certainly go out, if God wills," and "I will not go out except that God wills," is one. End of quote.

"Fa-taafa 'alayha ta'if": al-Nakha'i read it as "tiyf." Al-Farra' said: "al-ta'if" is a matter that comes by night. He refuted him with the words of God: ﴿When an evil whisper from Satan touches them﴾ (7:201), where it is not restricted to night, and "ta'if" is indefinite. It was said that it was Gabriel (peace be upon him), who uprooted it and circled it around the House, then placed it where the city of al-Ta'if is today, and for this reason it was named al-Ta'if; and there is no town in the land of the Hijaz that has water, trees and grapes except it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a visitation from your Lord's command. Qatada said: a punishment from your Lord. Ibn Jarir said: a tongue of fire that came out of the valley of Hell. "Fa-asbahat kal-sarim": Ibn 'Abbas said: like black ash; al-sarim is black ash in the dialect of Khuzayma. And from him also: al-sarim is a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing, and so their garden was compared to it. Al-Hasan said: "sarama 'anha al-khayr," meaning he cut off its good; so al-sarim has the sense of "masrum" (cut off). Al-Thawri said: like the dawn in that it had grown white, like a harvested field. Mu'arrij said: like a sand-dune that has been severed from the bulk of the sand, and a sand-dune does not produce anything of benefit. Al-Akhfash said: like the dawn that has been severed from the night. Al-Mubarrad said: like the day, with nothing in it. Shimr said: al-sarim is the night, and al-sarim is the day, meaning one is severed from the other. Al-Farra', Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id, and a group said: al-sarim is the night, in that their garden had turned black.

"Fa-tanadaw": they called to one another, urging each other to proceed to their appointment: "Go out early upon your tilth." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'go out to your tilth,' and what is the meaning of 'upon'? I answer: since going out to it was for the purpose of harvesting and cutting it, it became going out upon it, as you say: 'the enemy went out upon them.' It is also permissible that 'ghada' (go out early) be taken to include the sense of 'iqbal' (coming toward), as in their saying: 'he is brought food early and in the evening.' That is, come toward your tilth early in the morning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari assumed that "ghada" is transitive with "ila" (to), and that requires transmission (naql) in such a way that it is frequent, becoming the basis for it, and what contradicts it is interpreted. But what is in my memory is that it is transitive with "ala," as in the words of the poet:

I went out to him early in the morning and saw him
sitting upon him in al-Sarim, his blamers around him.

"In kuntum sarimin": the apparent meaning is that it is from the harvesting of palm trees. It was said: it may also mean: if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion, from your saying "a sharp sword" (sayf sarim).

"Yatakhafatun" (they whisper): they conceal their speech out of fear that the needy might perceive them. "An la yadkhulannaha" means: they whispered this statement, "No needy person shall enter it today." "An" is a verbal particle, and it may also be an explanatory particle. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "la yadkhulanna" without "an," either with the implied "yaqulun" (they say), or by treating "yatakhafatun" as equivalent to speech, since its meaning is "they speak secretly." The prohibition against entering is a prohibition against enabling it, meaning: do not enable them to enter, lest they enter.

"Wa ghadaw 'ala harding qadirin": that is, with intention and capability within themselves, thinking they had attained their goal. Ibn 'Abbas said this, meaning: heading to their garden swiftly, considering themselves capable of harvesting it. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: "'ala harding" means "upon prevention," meaning: capable within themselves of preventing the needy from its good. So God repaid them by preventing them from good. Al-Hasan said: "'ala harding" means in need and poverty. Al-Sudi and Sufyan said: "'ala harding" means in anger, meaning they were capable only of rage and anger toward one another. It was also said: "'ala harding" means "in isolation," meaning they went out alone without the needy. Al-Azhari said: "harding" is the name of their village. Al-Sudi said: it is the name of their garden, meaning they went out to that garden capable of harvesting it in their own estimation, or determining that their goal of harvesting would be accomplished for them. It was said that it may mean "taqdir" in the sense of constriction, based on God's words: ﴿and whoever has his provision restricted﴾ (65:7), meaning: constricting the needy, since they withheld from them what their father used to give them from it.

"Fa-lamma ra'awha": that is, in the condition in which they had set out upon it, from its destruction and the departure of its good, they said: "Indeed we have gone astray," meaning: we have lost the way to it. Qatada said this. At first they denied that it was it, and believed they had taken a wrong path to it; then it became clear to them that it was it, and that a punishment from God had befallen it that took away its good. It was also said: "Indeed we have gone astray" from the right course in our going out with the intention of preventing the needy. So they said: "Rather, we are deprived of its good through our betrayal of ourselves."

The most moderate of them said, meaning the best and most sound in judgment: "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify (God)?'" ﴿Why do you not glorify [God]?﴾ (68:28). He reprimanded and rebuked them for abandoning what he had urged upon them of glorifying God, that is, remembering Him and declaring Him free of imperfection. Had they remembered God and His kindness toward them, they would have complied with what He commanded of sharing with the needy and followed their father's practice in that. When they neglected the remembrance of God (exalted is He) and resolved to withhold from the needy, God tested them. This indicates that the most moderate of them had previously come to them and urged them to remember God (exalted is He). Mujahid and Abu Salih said: their exception was "Glory be to God." Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid made the glorification (tasbih) a substitute for "if God wills," because the meaning is declaring God free from anything occurring except by His will. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are united in the sense of glorifying God, since the exception is a committing of the matter to Him, and glorification is declaring Him free of imperfection, and each of committing and declaring free is an exaltation of Him. It was also said: "lawla tusabbihun" means "lawla tastaghfirun" (why do you not seek forgiveness?).

When he reprimanded them, they returned to the remembrance of God (exalted is He), acknowledged against themselves their wrongdoing, and hastened to glorify God (exalted is He), saying: "Glory be to our Lord." Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, we seek God's forgiveness for our sin. When they confessed their wrongdoing, some of them blamed others, and placed the blame on other than themselves, since among them there was one who adorned the plan, one who accepted it, one who ordered restraint, one who disobeyed the order, and one who remained silent with consent. Then they acknowledged that they had transgressed, and hoped, awaiting relief, that their Lord would give them in exchange something better than that garden: "Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it," meaning: in exchange for this garden, something better than it. The discussion of this has preceded in (the commentary on) al-Kahf, and the disagreement over the light and heavy pronunciation of "yubaddilana," as attributed to the readers, is known.

﴿Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire﴾ (68:32), meaning: we seek to receive good from Him. The apparent view is that the People of this garden were believers who committed a sin and repented. It was also said: they were from the People of the Book. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "It has reached me that the people called upon God and were sincere, and God knew from them the truth, so He gave them in exchange a garden, and every cluster of it was like a black-skinned man standing." From Mujahid: they repented, so they were given in exchange something better than it. Al-Qushayri said: most of them say that they repented and were sincere. End of quote. Al-Hasan hesitated about whether they were believers, and said: "Was their saying, 'Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire,' a (genuine) faith, or was it in the manner of the polytheists when hardship afflicts them?"

﴿Such is the punishment﴾ (68:33). This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the affair of Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reference by "such" is to the punishment that descended upon the Garden, that is, such is the punishment (that is), the one that descended upon Quraysh suddenly; then the punishment of the Hereafter after that is more severe for them than the punishment of this world. Many of the exegetes said: the punishment descended upon Quraysh, paralleling the affair of the Garden, is the drought that befell them for seven years, until they saw smoke and ate hides. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: like that punishment with which We tested the people of Mecca and the People of the Garden is the punishment of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and greater than it. End of quote.

The comparison of the trial of Quraysh with the trial of the People of the Garden is that the People of the Garden resolved to benefit from its fruit and deprive the needy, so God (exalted is He) turned it against them and deprived them. And when Quraysh went out to Badr, they swore to kill the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions; when they did that, they would return to Mecca, circle the Ka'ba, and drink wine, so God turned it against them by having them killed and captured. When He punished them with that in this world, He said: "And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 68, verse 7–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best﴾ is a warning to the astray, and they are, in reality, the madmen, since they had intellects which they did not benefit from and did not use for what the Messengers brought. Or ("knows best") may be a metaphor for the recompense of both groups. ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾, i.e., those who denied what Allah revealed to you of the Revelation. This is a prohibition against obeying them in anything of what they called him to, such as glorifying their gods. ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾: "law" (lau) here, according to the opinion of the Basrans, is a verbal particle with the meaning of "an" (that), i.e., they wish for your compromise. The discussion of this was mentioned in His – exalted is He – saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾. The view of the majority is that the object of "wadda" (wish) is omitted, i.e., they wish for your compromise, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, and "law" remains in its original sense as a conditional particle, meaning that what would have occurred did not occur because something else did not occur, and its answer is omitted, its estimated meaning being: they would have been pleased by that.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, ʿAtiyya and al-Suddi said: "law tudhin" means "law takfur" (if you were to disbelieve), so that they persist in their disbelief. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas as well: "if you were to be lenient with them, so they would be lenient with you." Qatada said: "if you were to turn away from this matter, so they would turn away with you." Al-Hasan said: "if you were to flatter them in your religion, so they would flatter you in their religion." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "if you were to be hypocritical and ostentatious, so they would be hypocritical with you and show off to you." Al-Rabi ibn Anas said: "if you were to lie, so they would lie." Abu Jaʿfar said: "if you were to weaken, so they would weaken." Al-Kalbi and al-Farra said: "if you were to soften, so they would soften." Aban ibn Thaʿlab said: "if you were to show favouritism, so they would be favoured." And they said other than these sayings.

Al-Farra said: "al-dihan" means softening (talyin). Al-Mufaddal said: hypocrisy and abandoning sincere advice. This is the transmission of the lexicographers, and what they said does not go beyond this, because what differs from this is an explanation by a necessary consequence. ﴿So they would compromise﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you would compromise﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He diverted it to another way, which is that it is made the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then they compromise", like His saying: ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord fears not﴾, meaning: they wish that you would compromise, so they then compromise, or they wish for your compromise, so they now compromise in hope of your compromise. End.

The majority of the codices have the nun. Harun said: in some codices it is ﴿fa-yudhinu﴾ (so that they compromise) with a naṣb (accusative), and for its accusative there are two possibilities: one is that it is the answer to "wadda" because it includes the meaning of "layta" (would that), and the second is that it is in the assumption that it was pronounced with "an", i.e., they wish that you would compromise so that they would compromise, so it is a coordination with the assumption. This second possibility does not arise except according to the view of the one who makes "law" a verbal particle with the meaning of "an".

﴿Do not obey every oath-taker, contemptible﴾. The explanation of "mahin" and what follows it was given earlier in the vocabulary (al-mufradat), and these attributes came as intensive forms (ṣifat mubalagha). The rhyme was observed in them, so ﴿ḥallaf﴾ (oath-taker) is followed by ﴿mahin﴾ (contemptible), because the nun in them with the mim is a kind of correspondence. Then came: ﴿hammaz, mashsha' bi-namim﴾ (a slanderer, going about with gossip), with the two intensive attributes (p-310). Then came: ﴿mannaʿ lil-khayr muʿtad athim﴾ (withholding from good, transgressing, sinful). So mannaʿ and athim are intensive attributes. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" (good) here is meant in its general sense, in whatever is called good. It was said: "khayr" here means wealth; he means one who withholds wealth, expressing by it stinginess. Its meaning: one who exceeds the limit in wrongdoing.

In the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, I said — meaning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — "What is the ʿutull, the zanim?" He said: "The one of wide belly, the one of ill-natured creation, the one who eats much and drinks much, the one who is cruel and wrongdoing." Al-Hasan read ʿutullin with a raised lam (ʿutullun), while the majority read it with a lowered lam after that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made his harshness and his arrogance his worst faults, because when he is harsh and his nature is coarse, his heart becomes hard, and he becomes bold toward every disobedience. Also, because it is generally the case that when a drop of semen is corrupt, the offspring from it becomes corrupt. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his child, nor his grandchild." And "after that" is in the sense of "then" in His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾. Al-Hasan read ʿutullun in the nominative, as a dispraise, and this reading strengthens what is indicated after that. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "after that" means: after we described him with it. So this order is only in the speech of the describer, not in the occurrence of those attributes in the one described; otherwise, his being ʿutull is prior to his being one who has wealth and withholds it. End.

"Zanim" means one who is attached to a people while not being from them, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others. It was also said: the zanim is the suspect, the one of ugly deeds. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the zanim is one who has a zanama (a growth) on his neck like the zanama of a sheep, and we did not know the one referred to until it was revealed, and we recognised him by his zanama. End.

It is reported that al-Akhnas ibn Sharif had this attribute; he had a zanama. Ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the zanim is the one known for evil, just as a sheep is known by its zanama. And also from him: that he is the one known for ignoble lineage. And also from him: that he is the wrongdoer. From ʿIkrima: he is the base. From Mujahid, ʿIkrima and Ibn al-Musayyab: that he is the child of fornication attached in lineage to the people. Al-Walid was a claimed son among Quraysh, not of their stock; his father claimed him eighteen years after his birth. Mujahid said: he had six fingers on his hand, with an extra finger on each thumb.

What appears is that these attributes are not specific to one individual. Do you not see His saying: ﴿every oath-taker﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed We have tested them﴾? The prohibition was only against obeying one who has these attributes.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said, summarized: The two Nahwis, the two Harams, Hafs and the people of Madina read ﴿an kana﴾ as a statement; the rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Jaʿfar read it as a question. Hamza made both hamzas clear, and the rest eased the second. As for the statement reading, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that ʿutull act upon it, even though it has been described. End. This is the view of the Kufans, and it is not permissible according to the Basrans. It was also said: "zanim" (in the sense of "an kana" with "zanim") especially according to the view of the one who interpreted it as "ill-natured in deeds."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying "do not obey", i.e., do not obey him with these faults, because he has wealth, i.e., because of his affluence and his share of this world. It is also permissible that it is connected to what follows it, in the sense of: because he is one who has wealth and is supported by sons, ﴿he denies Our signs﴾, and it does not act upon it. The one who is the answer of "idha" (when)… because what follows the condition does not act upon what precedes it, but what the sentence indicates of the meaning of denial. End.

As for the interrogative reading, it is possible that a verb is supplied which is indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he be obeyed because he has wealth?" Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "would you obey him because he has wealth?" Or a verb indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he deny or deny outright because he has wealth?"

Nafi, in the narration of al-Yazidi from him, read ﴿in kana﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: the condition is addressed to the addressee, i.e., do not obey every oath-taker making his affluence a condition; because when he obeys the disbeliever for his wealth, it is as if he made affluence a condition of obedience. Directing the condition to the addressee is like directing the hope to him in His saying: ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾. End.

And the sayings: "an kana" is a condition, and "idha tutla" is a condition; so this is a case where two conditions are combined, and they are not among the conditions whose occurrence is ordered. The one that comes later in wording is the one that comes first, and the one that comes first in wording is a condition for the second, as in his verse:

"If I stumble after this, if my soul is drawn from here, then say: no, no."

Because what prevents attention to the signs of Allah is his having wealth and sons; he is preoccupied in heart, so he is heedless of reflection and thought. The world has taken hold of him and made him insolent.

Al-Hasan read ﴿a-idha﴾ as an interrogative, and it is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach for his saying: "The Qur'an is the fables of the ancients", when the signs of Allah were recited to him. When he mentioned his evil deeds and sayings, he mentioned what will be done to him by way of threat, saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. The branding is the mark.

Since the face is the noblest part of man, and the nose is the most honoured of the face because it is foremost, for this reason they made it the place of might and zeal, and derived from it the word "anafa" (pride), and they said: "one with zealous nose, lofty of the bridge"; and of the humiliated they said: "his nose was cut off" and "his nose was rubbed in the dust." It was also a place where marks appear for elevation. He said: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾, and this is the utmost of humiliation, contempt and enslavement, since he became like a beast which cannot repel its branding on the nose. If branding on the face is a disfigurement, how much more so on the most honoured limb of it? It has been said: beauty is in the nose; and some men of letters said:

"The beauty of a young man is in the nose, and the nose is bare, so how is it when the mole becomes an ornament for it?"

﴿We shall brand him﴾ is a future verb whose time is not fixed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is striking with the sword, i.e., he is struck on his face and on his nose, so that will be like branding on the nose, and that happened to him on the day of Badr. Al-Mubarrad said: that is in the punishment of the Hereafter, in Jahannam, and it is torment by fire on their noses. Others said: that is on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., we shall brand his nose with a mark by which his disbelief and the lowering of his rank will be recognised. Qatada and others said: its meaning is that We shall do to him in this world of blame, hatred and notoriety for evil what will remain on him and not be hidden, so that will be like a branding on the nose, firm and clear, as you say: "I shall put a collar on you like the collar of the dove", meaning: I shall make the matter clear in you. In this sense Jarir meant by his saying:

"When I placed my branding-iron upon al-Farazdaq"

In branding on the nose there is disfigurement, so its metaphorical use for dispraised things came highly eloquent. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: If you consider the state of Abu Jahl and his like, and what was established for them in this world of evil consequences in the Hereafter, you will see that they were branded on the snouts. End. Abu al-ʿAliya and Muqatil, and al-Farra preferred it, said: his face will blacken before entering the Fire, and He mentioned the snout, while the intended meaning is the face, because part of the face stands for part of it. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: The disbeliever only went to extremes in enmity to the Messenger (ﷺ) because of pride and zeal; so, since the witness of rejection is pride and zeal, He expressed this specificity by His saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. End of his words. In using "khurtum" (snout) in place of "anf" (nose) there is contempt and disdain, because the true meaning of "khurtum" belongs to beasts of prey.

It is concluded from this whether His saying "We shall brand him upon the snout" is literal or metaphorical; and if it is literal, is that in this world or in the Hereafter? Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, in his tafsir, went far in interpreting "khurtum" as wine, meaning: We shall flog him for drinking it.

When he described those who possess these blameworthy qualities, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh, He (exalted is He) informed them of what befell them of trial through drought and hunger, in response to the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Joseph," the hadith in full. (This was) like how We tested the People of the Garden, whose story was known to them. It was a garden in the land of Yemen, at San'a, belonging to a man who used to pay God's due from it. When he died it passed to his son, and they withheld its bounty from the people and were stingy with God's due, so God (exalted is He) destroyed it from a direction they could not repel what had befallen them. It was also said: it was at Suran, a few farsakhs from San'a, belonging to a people after the raising of Jesus (peace be upon him). Its owner used to give to the needy what the sickle missed, what lay at the bottom of the heaps, what the grape-picking missed, and what remained on the palm-fronds under the palm tree when it was harvested. A great deal would gather for them. When he died his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will become constrained for us, and we have dependents." So they swore that they would harvest it at dawn in the darkness, secretly from the needy, and they did not make an exception in their oath.

The kaf in "kama" (as) is in the accusative position, and "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. It was also said: "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and "idh" is the object of "balawnahum" (We tested them). "Layasrimunnaha" is the answer to the oath, not a quotation of their own words, for had it been their words it would have been "lanasrimanna" with the first-person plural. The meaning: they would certainly gather its fruit when they entered in the morning, before the needy came out in their usual habit with their father. "Wa la yastathnun" means: they did not turn back from what they had resolved upon of denying the needy. Mujahid said: its meaning is that they did not say "if God wills," but resolved upon that with the resolve of one who controls his own affair. Al-Zamakhshari, following Mujahid's view, said: "nor did they say, 'if God wills.'" (If you ask) why is it called an exception (istithna') when it is only a condition (shart)? (I answer): because it performs the function of an exception, since the meaning of your saying, "I will certainly go out, if God wills," and "I will not go out except that God wills," is one. End of quote.

"Fa-taafa 'alayha ta'if": al-Nakha'i read it as "tiyf." Al-Farra' said: "al-ta'if" is a matter that comes by night. He refuted him with the words of God: ﴿When an evil whisper from Satan touches them﴾ (7:201), where it is not restricted to night, and "ta'if" is indefinite. It was said that it was Gabriel (peace be upon him), who uprooted it and circled it around the House, then placed it where the city of al-Ta'if is today, and for this reason it was named al-Ta'if; and there is no town in the land of the Hijaz that has water, trees and grapes except it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a visitation from your Lord's command. Qatada said: a punishment from your Lord. Ibn Jarir said: a tongue of fire that came out of the valley of Hell. "Fa-asbahat kal-sarim": Ibn 'Abbas said: like black ash; al-sarim is black ash in the dialect of Khuzayma. And from him also: al-sarim is a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing, and so their garden was compared to it. Al-Hasan said: "sarama 'anha al-khayr," meaning he cut off its good; so al-sarim has the sense of "masrum" (cut off). Al-Thawri said: like the dawn in that it had grown white, like a harvested field. Mu'arrij said: like a sand-dune that has been severed from the bulk of the sand, and a sand-dune does not produce anything of benefit. Al-Akhfash said: like the dawn that has been severed from the night. Al-Mubarrad said: like the day, with nothing in it. Shimr said: al-sarim is the night, and al-sarim is the day, meaning one is severed from the other. Al-Farra', Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id, and a group said: al-sarim is the night, in that their garden had turned black.

"Fa-tanadaw": they called to one another, urging each other to proceed to their appointment: "Go out early upon your tilth." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'go out to your tilth,' and what is the meaning of 'upon'? I answer: since going out to it was for the purpose of harvesting and cutting it, it became going out upon it, as you say: 'the enemy went out upon them.' It is also permissible that 'ghada' (go out early) be taken to include the sense of 'iqbal' (coming toward), as in their saying: 'he is brought food early and in the evening.' That is, come toward your tilth early in the morning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari assumed that "ghada" is transitive with "ila" (to), and that requires transmission (naql) in such a way that it is frequent, becoming the basis for it, and what contradicts it is interpreted. But what is in my memory is that it is transitive with "ala," as in the words of the poet:

I went out to him early in the morning and saw him
sitting upon him in al-Sarim, his blamers around him.

"In kuntum sarimin": the apparent meaning is that it is from the harvesting of palm trees. It was said: it may also mean: if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion, from your saying "a sharp sword" (sayf sarim).

"Yatakhafatun" (they whisper): they conceal their speech out of fear that the needy might perceive them. "An la yadkhulannaha" means: they whispered this statement, "No needy person shall enter it today." "An" is a verbal particle, and it may also be an explanatory particle. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "la yadkhulanna" without "an," either with the implied "yaqulun" (they say), or by treating "yatakhafatun" as equivalent to speech, since its meaning is "they speak secretly." The prohibition against entering is a prohibition against enabling it, meaning: do not enable them to enter, lest they enter.

"Wa ghadaw 'ala harding qadirin": that is, with intention and capability within themselves, thinking they had attained their goal. Ibn 'Abbas said this, meaning: heading to their garden swiftly, considering themselves capable of harvesting it. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: "'ala harding" means "upon prevention," meaning: capable within themselves of preventing the needy from its good. So God repaid them by preventing them from good. Al-Hasan said: "'ala harding" means in need and poverty. Al-Sudi and Sufyan said: "'ala harding" means in anger, meaning they were capable only of rage and anger toward one another. It was also said: "'ala harding" means "in isolation," meaning they went out alone without the needy. Al-Azhari said: "harding" is the name of their village. Al-Sudi said: it is the name of their garden, meaning they went out to that garden capable of harvesting it in their own estimation, or determining that their goal of harvesting would be accomplished for them. It was said that it may mean "taqdir" in the sense of constriction, based on God's words: ﴿and whoever has his provision restricted﴾ (65:7), meaning: constricting the needy, since they withheld from them what their father used to give them from it.

"Fa-lamma ra'awha": that is, in the condition in which they had set out upon it, from its destruction and the departure of its good, they said: "Indeed we have gone astray," meaning: we have lost the way to it. Qatada said this. At first they denied that it was it, and believed they had taken a wrong path to it; then it became clear to them that it was it, and that a punishment from God had befallen it that took away its good. It was also said: "Indeed we have gone astray" from the right course in our going out with the intention of preventing the needy. So they said: "Rather, we are deprived of its good through our betrayal of ourselves."

The most moderate of them said, meaning the best and most sound in judgment: "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify (God)?'" ﴿Why do you not glorify [God]?﴾ (68:28). He reprimanded and rebuked them for abandoning what he had urged upon them of glorifying God, that is, remembering Him and declaring Him free of imperfection. Had they remembered God and His kindness toward them, they would have complied with what He commanded of sharing with the needy and followed their father's practice in that. When they neglected the remembrance of God (exalted is He) and resolved to withhold from the needy, God tested them. This indicates that the most moderate of them had previously come to them and urged them to remember God (exalted is He). Mujahid and Abu Salih said: their exception was "Glory be to God." Al-Nahhas said: Mujahid made the glorification (tasbih) a substitute for "if God wills," because the meaning is declaring God free from anything occurring except by His will. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are united in the sense of glorifying God, since the exception is a committing of the matter to Him, and glorification is declaring Him free of imperfection, and each of committing and declaring free is an exaltation of Him. It was also said: "lawla tusabbihun" means "lawla tastaghfirun" (why do you not seek forgiveness?).

When he reprimanded them, they returned to the remembrance of God (exalted is He), acknowledged against themselves their wrongdoing, and hastened to glorify God (exalted is He), saying: "Glory be to our Lord." Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, we seek God's forgiveness for our sin. When they confessed their wrongdoing, some of them blamed others, and placed the blame on other than themselves, since among them there was one who adorned the plan, one who accepted it, one who ordered restraint, one who disobeyed the order, and one who remained silent with consent. Then they acknowledged that they had transgressed, and hoped, awaiting relief, that their Lord would give them in exchange something better than that garden: "Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it," meaning: in exchange for this garden, something better than it. The discussion of this has preceded in (the commentary on) al-Kahf, and the disagreement over the light and heavy pronunciation of "yubaddilana," as attributed to the readers, is known.

﴿Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire﴾ (68:32), meaning: we seek to receive good from Him. The apparent view is that the People of this garden were believers who committed a sin and repented. It was also said: they were from the People of the Book. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: "It has reached me that the people called upon God and were sincere, and God knew from them the truth, so He gave them in exchange a garden, and every cluster of it was like a black-skinned man standing." From Mujahid: they repented, so they were given in exchange something better than it. Al-Qushayri said: most of them say that they repented and were sincere. End of quote. Al-Hasan hesitated about whether they were believers, and said: "Was their saying, 'Indeed we turn to our Lord in desire,' a (genuine) faith, or was it in the manner of the polytheists when hardship afflicts them?"

﴿Such is the punishment﴾ (68:33). This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the affair of Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the reference by "such" is to the punishment that descended upon the Garden, that is, such is the punishment (that is), the one that descended upon Quraysh suddenly; then the punishment of the Hereafter after that is more severe for them than the punishment of this world. Many of the exegetes said: the punishment descended upon Quraysh, paralleling the affair of the Garden, is the drought that befell them for seven years, until they saw smoke and ate hides. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari said: like that punishment with which We tested the people of Mecca and the People of the Garden is the punishment of this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and greater than it. End of quote.

The comparison of the trial of Quraysh with the trial of the People of the Garden is that the People of the Garden resolved to benefit from its fruit and deprive the needy, so God (exalted is He) turned it against them and deprived them. And when Quraysh went out to Badr, they swore to kill the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions; when they did that, they would return to Mecca, circle the Ka'ba, and drink wine, so God turned it against them by having them killed and captured. When He punished them with that in this world, He said: "And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 68, verse 7–33 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows best﴾ is a warning to the astray, and they are, in reality, the madmen, since they had intellects which they did not benefit from and did not use for what the Messengers brought. Or ("knows best") may be a metaphor for the recompense of both groups. ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾, i.e., those who denied what Allah revealed to you of the Revelation. This is a prohibition against obeying them in anything of what they called him to, such as glorifying their gods. ﴿They wish you would compromise﴾: "law" (lau) here, according to the opinion of the Basrans, is a verbal particle with the meaning of "an" (that), i.e., they wish for your compromise. The discussion of this was mentioned in His – exalted is He – saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾. The view of the majority is that the object of "wadda" (wish) is omitted, i.e., they wish for your compromise, and it was omitted because what follows indicates it, and "law" remains in its original sense as a conditional particle, meaning that what would have occurred did not occur because something else did not occur, and its answer is omitted, its estimated meaning being: they would have been pleased by that.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, ʿAtiyya and al-Suddi said: "law tudhin" means "law takfur" (if you were to disbelieve), so that they persist in their disbelief. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas as well: "if you were to be lenient with them, so they would be lenient with you." Qatada said: "if you were to turn away from this matter, so they would turn away with you." Al-Hasan said: "if you were to flatter them in your religion, so they would flatter you in their religion." Zayd ibn Aslam said: "if you were to be hypocritical and ostentatious, so they would be hypocritical with you and show off to you." Al-Rabi ibn Anas said: "if you were to lie, so they would lie." Abu Jaʿfar said: "if you were to weaken, so they would weaken." Al-Kalbi and al-Farra said: "if you were to soften, so they would soften." Aban ibn Thaʿlab said: "if you were to show favouritism, so they would be favoured." And they said other than these sayings.

Al-Farra said: "al-dihan" means softening (talyin). Al-Mufaddal said: hypocrisy and abandoning sincere advice. This is the transmission of the lexicographers, and what they said does not go beyond this, because what differs from this is an explanation by a necessary consequence. ﴿So they would compromise﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you would compromise﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He diverted it to another way, which is that it is made the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "then they compromise", like His saying: ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord fears not﴾, meaning: they wish that you would compromise, so they then compromise, or they wish for your compromise, so they now compromise in hope of your compromise. End.

The majority of the codices have the nun. Harun said: in some codices it is ﴿fa-yudhinu﴾ (so that they compromise) with a naṣb (accusative), and for its accusative there are two possibilities: one is that it is the answer to "wadda" because it includes the meaning of "layta" (would that), and the second is that it is in the assumption that it was pronounced with "an", i.e., they wish that you would compromise so that they would compromise, so it is a coordination with the assumption. This second possibility does not arise except according to the view of the one who makes "law" a verbal particle with the meaning of "an".

﴿Do not obey every oath-taker, contemptible﴾. The explanation of "mahin" and what follows it was given earlier in the vocabulary (al-mufradat), and these attributes came as intensive forms (ṣifat mubalagha). The rhyme was observed in them, so ﴿ḥallaf﴾ (oath-taker) is followed by ﴿mahin﴾ (contemptible), because the nun in them with the mim is a kind of correspondence. Then came: ﴿hammaz, mashsha' bi-namim﴾ (a slanderer, going about with gossip), with the two intensive attributes (p-310). Then came: ﴿mannaʿ lil-khayr muʿtad athim﴾ (withholding from good, transgressing, sinful). So mannaʿ and athim are intensive attributes. The apparent meaning is that "khayr" (good) here is meant in its general sense, in whatever is called good. It was said: "khayr" here means wealth; he means one who withholds wealth, expressing by it stinginess. Its meaning: one who exceeds the limit in wrongdoing.

In the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws, I said — meaning to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) — "What is the ʿutull, the zanim?" He said: "The one of wide belly, the one of ill-natured creation, the one who eats much and drinks much, the one who is cruel and wrongdoing." Al-Hasan read ʿutullin with a raised lam (ʿutullun), while the majority read it with a lowered lam after that.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made his harshness and his arrogance his worst faults, because when he is harsh and his nature is coarse, his heart becomes hard, and he becomes bold toward every disobedience. Also, because it is generally the case that when a drop of semen is corrupt, the offspring from it becomes corrupt. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his child, nor his grandchild." And "after that" is in the sense of "then" in His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾. Al-Hasan read ʿutullun in the nominative, as a dispraise, and this reading strengthens what is indicated after that. End.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "after that" means: after we described him with it. So this order is only in the speech of the describer, not in the occurrence of those attributes in the one described; otherwise, his being ʿutull is prior to his being one who has wealth and withholds it. End.

"Zanim" means one who is attached to a people while not being from them, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others. It was also said: the zanim is the suspect, the one of ugly deeds. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: the zanim is one who has a zanama (a growth) on his neck like the zanama of a sheep, and we did not know the one referred to until it was revealed, and we recognised him by his zanama. End.

It is reported that al-Akhnas ibn Sharif had this attribute; he had a zanama. Ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the zanim is the one known for evil, just as a sheep is known by its zanama. And also from him: that he is the one known for ignoble lineage. And also from him: that he is the wrongdoer. From ʿIkrima: he is the base. From Mujahid, ʿIkrima and Ibn al-Musayyab: that he is the child of fornication attached in lineage to the people. Al-Walid was a claimed son among Quraysh, not of their stock; his father claimed him eighteen years after his birth. Mujahid said: he had six fingers on his hand, with an extra finger on each thumb.

What appears is that these attributes are not specific to one individual. Do you not see His saying: ﴿every oath-taker﴾ and His saying: ﴿Indeed We have tested them﴾? The prohibition was only against obeying one who has these attributes.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said, summarized: The two Nahwis, the two Harams, Hafs and the people of Madina read ﴿an kana﴾ as a statement; the rest of the seven, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Jaʿfar read it as a question. Hamza made both hamzas clear, and the rest eased the second. As for the statement reading, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is permissible that ʿutull act upon it, even though it has been described. End. This is the view of the Kufans, and it is not permissible according to the Basrans. It was also said: "zanim" (in the sense of "an kana" with "zanim") especially according to the view of the one who interpreted it as "ill-natured in deeds."

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying "do not obey", i.e., do not obey him with these faults, because he has wealth, i.e., because of his affluence and his share of this world. It is also permissible that it is connected to what follows it, in the sense of: because he is one who has wealth and is supported by sons, ﴿he denies Our signs﴾, and it does not act upon it. The one who is the answer of "idha" (when)… because what follows the condition does not act upon what precedes it, but what the sentence indicates of the meaning of denial. End.

As for the interrogative reading, it is possible that a verb is supplied which is indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he be obeyed because he has wealth?" Al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "would you obey him because he has wealth?" Or a verb indicated by what precedes it, i.e., "would he deny or deny outright because he has wealth?"

Nafi, in the narration of al-Yazidi from him, read ﴿in kana﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Zamakhshari said: the condition is addressed to the addressee, i.e., do not obey every oath-taker making his affluence a condition; because when he obeys the disbeliever for his wealth, it is as if he made affluence a condition of obedience. Directing the condition to the addressee is like directing the hope to him in His saying: ﴿perhaps he will remember﴾. End.

And the sayings: "an kana" is a condition, and "idha tutla" is a condition; so this is a case where two conditions are combined, and they are not among the conditions whose occurrence is ordered. The one that comes later in wording is the one that comes first, and the one that comes first in wording is a condition for the second, as in his verse:

"If I stumble after this, if my soul is drawn from here, then say: no, no."

Because what prevents attention to the signs of Allah is his having wealth and sons; he is preoccupied in heart, so he is heedless of reflection and thought. The world has taken hold of him and made him insolent.

Al-Hasan read ﴿a-idha﴾ as an interrogative, and it is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach for his saying: "The Qur'an is the fables of the ancients", when the signs of Allah were recited to him. When he mentioned his evil deeds and sayings, he mentioned what will be done to him by way of threat, saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. The branding is the mark.

Since the face is the noblest part of man, and the nose is the most honoured of the face because it is foremost, for this reason they made it the place of might and zeal, and derived from it the word "anafa" (pride), and they said: "one with zealous nose, lofty of the bridge"; and of the humiliated they said: "his nose was cut off" and "his nose was rubbed in the dust." It was also a place where marks appear for elevation. He said: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾, and this is the utmost of humiliation, contempt and enslavement, since he became like a beast which cannot repel its branding on the nose. If branding on the face is a disfigurement, how much more so on the most honoured limb of it? It has been said: beauty is in the nose; and some men of letters said:

"The beauty of a young man is in the nose, and the nose is bare, so how is it when the mole becomes an ornament for it?"

﴿We shall brand him﴾ is a future verb whose time is not fixed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is striking with the sword, i.e., he is struck on his face and on his nose, so that will be like branding on the nose, and that happened to him on the day of Badr. Al-Mubarrad said: that is in the punishment of the Hereafter, in Jahannam, and it is torment by fire on their noses. Others said: that is on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., we shall brand his nose with a mark by which his disbelief and the lowering of his rank will be recognised. Qatada and others said: its meaning is that We shall do to him in this world of blame, hatred and notoriety for evil what will remain on him and not be hidden, so that will be like a branding on the nose, firm and clear, as you say: "I shall put a collar on you like the collar of the dove", meaning: I shall make the matter clear in you. In this sense Jarir meant by his saying:

"When I placed my branding-iron upon al-Farazdaq"

In branding on the nose there is disfigurement, so its metaphorical use for dispraised things came highly eloquent. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: If you consider the state of Abu Jahl and his like, and what was established for them in this world of evil consequences in the Hereafter, you will see that they were branded on the snouts. End. Abu al-ʿAliya and Muqatil, and al-Farra preferred it, said: his face will blacken before entering the Fire, and He mentioned the snout, while the intended meaning is the face, because part of the face stands for part of it. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: The disbeliever only went to extremes in enmity to the Messenger (ﷺ) because of pride and zeal; so, since the witness of rejection is pride and zeal, He expressed this specificity by His saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout﴾. End of his words. In using "khurtum" (snout) in place of "anf" (nose) there is contempt and disdain, because the true meaning of "khurtum" belongs to beasts of prey.

It is concluded from this whether His saying "We shall brand him upon the snout" is literal or metaphorical; and if it is literal, is that in this world or in the Hereafter? Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, in his tafsir, went far in interpreting "khurtum" as wine, meaning: We shall flog him for drinking it.

When he described those who possess these blameworthy qualities, who are the disbelievers of Quraysh, He (exalted is He) informed them of what befell them of trial through drought and hunger, in response to the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "O God, tighten Your grip upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Joseph," the hadith in full. (This was) like how We tested the People of the Garden, whose story was known to them. It was a garden in the land of Yemen, at San'a, belonging to a man who used to pay God's due from it. When he died it passed to his son, and they withheld its bounty from the people and were stingy with God's due, so God (exalted is He) destroyed it from a direction they could not repel what had befallen them. It was also said: it was at Suran, a few farsakhs from San'a, belonging to a people after the raising of Jesus (peace be upon him). Its owner used to give to the needy what the sickle missed, what lay at the bottom of the heaps, what the grape-picking missed, and what remained on the palm-fronds under the palm tree when it was harvested. A great deal would gather for them. When he died his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will become constrained for us, and we have dependents." So they swore that they would harvest it at dawn in the darkness, secretly from the needy, and they did not make an exception in their oath.

The kaf in "kama" (as) is in the accusative position, and "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. It was also said: "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), and "idh" is the object of "balawnahum" (We tested them). "Layasrimunnaha" is the answer to the oath, not a quotation of their own words, for had it been their words it would have been "lanasrimanna" with the first-person plural. The meaning: they would certainly gather its fruit when they entered in the morning, before the needy came out in their usual habit with their father. "Wa la yastathnun" means: they did not turn back from what they had resolved upon of denying the needy. Mujahid said: its meaning is that they did not say "if God wills," but resolved upon that with the resolve of one who controls his own affair. Al-Zamakhshari, following Mujahid's view, said: "nor did they say, 'if God wills.'" (If you ask) why is it called an exception (istithna') when it is only a condition (shart)? (I answer): because it performs the function of an exception, since the meaning of your saying, "I will certainly go out, if God wills," and "I will not go out except that God wills," is one. End of quote.

"Fa-taafa 'alayha ta'if": al-Nakha'i read it as "tiyf." Al-Farra' said: "al-ta'if" is a matter that comes by night. He refuted him with the words of God: ﴿When an evil whisper from Satan touches them﴾ (7:201), where it is not restricted to night, and "ta'if" is indefinite. It was said that it was Gabriel (peace be upon him), who uprooted it and circled it around the House, then placed it where the city of al-Ta'if is today, and for this reason it was named al-Ta'if; and there is no town in the land of the Hijaz that has water, trees and grapes except it. Ibn 'Abbas said: a visitation from your Lord's command. Qatada said: a punishment from your Lord. Ibn Jarir said: a tongue of fire that came out of the valley of Hell. "Fa-asbahat kal-sarim": Ibn 'Abbas said: like black ash; al-sarim is black ash in the dialect of Khuzayma. And from him also: al-sarim is a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that produces nothing, and so their garden was compared to it. Al-Hasan said: "sarama 'anha al-khayr," meaning he cut off its good; so al-sarim has the sense of "masrum" (cut off). Al-Thawri said: like the dawn in that it had grown white, like a harvested field. Mu'arrij said: like a sand-dune that has been severed from the bulk of the sand, and a sand-dune does not produce anything of benefit. Al-Akhfash said: like the dawn that has been severed from the night. Al-Mubarrad said: like the day, with nothing in it. Shimr said: al-sarim is the night, and al-sarim is the day, meaning one is severed from the other. Al-Farra', Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id, and a group said: al-sarim is the night, in that their garden had turned black.

"Fa-tanadaw": they called to one another, urging each other to proceed to their appointment: "Go out early upon your tilth." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, why was it not said 'go out to your tilth,' and what is the meaning of 'upon'? I answer: since going out to it was for the purpose of harvesting and cutting it, it became going out upon it, as you say: 'the enemy went out upon them.' It is also permissible that 'ghada' (go out early) be taken to include the sense of 'iqbal' (coming toward), as in their saying: 'he is brought food early and in the evening.' That is, come toward your tilth early in the morning." End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari assumed that "ghada" is transitive with "ila" (to), and that requires transmission (naql) in such a way that it is frequent, becoming the basis for it, and what contradicts it is interpreted. But what is in my memory is that it is transitive with "ala," as in the words of the poet:

I went out to him early in the morning and saw him
sitting upon him in al-Sarim, his blamers around him.

"In kuntum sarimin": the apparent meaning is that it is from the harvesting of palm trees. It was said: it may also mean: if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion, from your saying "a sharp sword" (sayf sarim).

"Yatakhafatun" (they whisper): they conceal their speech out of fear that the needy might perceive them. "An la yadkhulannaha" means: they whispered this statement, "No needy person shall enter it today." "An" is a verbal particle, and it may also be an explanatory particle. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "la yadkhulanna" without "an," either with the implied "yaqulun" (they say), or by treating "yatakhafatun" as equivalent to speech, since its meaning is "they speak secretly." The prohibition against entering is a prohibition against enabling it, meaning: do not enable them to enter, lest they enter.

"Wa ghadaw 'ala harding qadirin": that is, with intention and capability within themselves, thinking they had attained their goal. Ibn 'Abbas said this, meaning: heading to their garden swiftly, considering themselves capable of harvesting it. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi said: "'ala harding" means "upon prevention," meaning: capable within themselves of preventing the needy from its good. So God repaid them by preventing them from good. Al-Hasan said: "'ala harding" means in need and poverty. Al-Sudi and Sufyan said: "'ala harding" means in anger, meaning they were capable only of rage and anger toward one another. It was also said: "'ala harding" means "in isolation," meaning they went out alone without the needy. Al-Azhari said: "harding" is the name of their village. Al-Sudi said: it is the name of their garden, meaning they went out to that garden capable of harvesting it in their own estimation, or determining that their goal of harvesting would be accomplished for them.
