It was said that in both readings the intended meaning is the idols, or people who share with them in their saying and agree with them in it, meaning: no one says what they say, just as they have no Book, no covenant from Allah, and no guarantor for this. So let them bring their partners. This is a summons and an inquiry. It was said: in this world, meaning let them bring them forth so that you see whether they are like those who harm and benefit or not. It was said: in the Hereafter, that they should bring them.

﴿On a Day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. According to this view, the one who governs the "day" is "let them bring." It was also said: remember (udhkur). It was also said the estimate is: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered, there will be such and such," and it was omitted for the great awe of what will happen in it of events. The apparent meaning, and the view of the majority, is that this Day is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim said: this Day is in this world, because He said: "and they will be called to prostration," and the Day of Resurrection contains no worship or obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is either the last days of a person's life in this world, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news﴾ [al-Furqan: 22], then he sees people called to prayer when its times come, but he cannot pray, because it is the time when faith will not benefit a soul. Or it refers to the state of illness, old age and infirmity. "And they used to be called to prostration before that day while they were sound," from what they now have. That is either because of the severity of the calamity upon them from the terror of what they witnessed at death, or from weakness and old age. It is answered that the calling to prostration is not by way of obligation, but by way of rebuke and humiliation. When they are called to prostration, they are deprived of the ability to do it, and power is withheld from them, so that their grief and regret over what they neglected when they were called to it, while their limbs and joints were sound, will increase.

The majority read "yukshafu" with a ya' in the passive voice. Abd Allah ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud also, and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a nun. Ibn Abbas read "yakshifu" with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. He also read it with a ya' with a damma in the passive voice. It was read "yukshifu" with a ya' with a damma and a kasra on the shin, from ak-shafa, when one enters into uncovering (kashf); from it: "ak-shafa al-rajul" meaning his upper lip retracted. The uncovering of the shin is a metaphor for the severity of the matter and its intensification. Mujahid said: it is the first hour of the Day of Resurrection, and it is the most terrible of them. What came in the hadith in His saying: "Then He will uncover for them the shin," is also to be understood as referring to severity on that Day, and it is a common metaphor in the language of the Arabs. Hatim said:

"A man of war, if war bites him, he bites it back, and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up as well."

And the rajaz poet said:

"I marvel at myself and at her concern, and at my chasing the horses from their provisions,
In a year that has uncovered its shin, red, stripping the flesh from its bones."

And the rajaz poet said:

"It has rolled up its shin, so tighten your grip; war has come upon you, so strive."

And another said:

"Patience before me, if evil remains; war has stood with us upon its shin."

And the poet said:

"It has uncovered its shin for them, and the calamities of evil have appeared."

It is also narrated as "al-Sudah." Ibn Abbas said: "on a Day when there is uncovering of a severe matter." Abu Ubaydah said: this is a word used for severity; it is said: "He uncovered his shin" when he rolled up his garment. He said: from this the Arabs say of a year of drought: "it has uncovered its shin." He made "shin" indefinite to indicate that it is an undefined matter of severity, outside the familiar, like His saying: ﴿On the Day when the caller calls to a thing unknown﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. It is as if it were said: "On a Day when a terrible, overwhelming matter occurs."

﴿And they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. Its apparent meaning is that they are called, and it has been mentioned that this is by way of rebuke, not by way of obligation. It was said: the caller is what they see of the prostration of believers, so they wish to prostrate but cannot, as occurs in the hadith in which Allah dialogues with them, that they say: "You are our Lord," and they fall down in prostration, so every believer prostrates, and the backs of the hypocrites and disbelievers become like cow-horns, one bone, so they are unable to prostrate. End of quotation. The negation of ability to prostrate in the Hereafter does not indicate that they have ability in this world, as al-Jubba'i held.

﴿Humbled (khashi'ah) their eyes﴾: a circumstantial state (hal), the subject of which is the pronoun in "they are called." He specified the eyes with humility, although all the limbs will be humble, because it is clearer in them than in every other limb. ﴿Humiliation will cover them (tarhaquhum)﴾ meaning: will overwhelm them, ﴿while they were being called to prostration﴾. It was said: this is an expression for all acts of obedience, and it was specified by mention because it is the greatest of acts of obedience, and because they were tested with it in the Hereafter. Al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi said: by prostration is meant the obligatory prayers. Ibn Jubayr said: they used to hear the call to prayer and "come to success," and they did not respond.

﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this message﴾. The meaning: leave Me to deal with him, for I will requite him, and there is no one to prevent Me. This is a severe threat to whoever denies what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought concerning the matter of the Hereafter and other things, and Allah, the Exalted, had already presented matters concerning the states of the happy and the wretched. "And whoever" (man) is in a place of accusative, either as a conjunction (ma'tuf) on the pronoun in "leave Me," or as an object with (maf'ul ma'ah). ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed My plan is firm﴾: it has been discussed in al-A'raf. ﴿Or do you ask them for payment, so they are burdened with debt﴾ up to ﴿write﴾: it has been discussed in al-Tur.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to invoke curse upon those who fled at Uhud when the matter became severe for the Muslims. It was also said: when he wanted to invoke curse upon Thaqif, and so this was revealed: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾, meaning: His granting them respite and delaying your victory over them, and proceed with what you were commanded of conveying the message and bearing harm. ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾: this is Yunus (peace be upon him), ﴿when he called out﴾, meaning: in the belly of the fish, and this is his saying: "There is no god but You; glory be to You." The prohibition is not directed at the persons themselves; rather the meaning is: let your condition not be like his condition. "When he called out": the governing element of "when" (idh) is the omitted noun to which it is attached, meaning: like the condition of, or like the story of, the companion of the fish when he called out. ﴿While he was suppressing (makzum)﴾: filled with anger against his people, since they did not believe when he invited them to faith, and they compelled him to hasten leaving them. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"And you, from love of Mayy, conceal a sorrow, afflicted in heart, anguished, suppressing, heavy in heart."

The root *k-ẓ-m* was already discussed in His words: ﴿and those who restrain their anger﴾. Most readers recite ﴿tadārakahu﴾ (his Lord's favour "reached" him) as a past-tense verb, without the feminine marker (*ta' al-ta'nīth*), in order to improve the separation between the verb and its subject. ʿAbdullah and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿tadārakathu﴾ with the feminine *tā'*. Ibn Hurmuz, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read it with a doubled *dāl* (*tadārrakahu*). Abu Hatim said: "This is not permissible. The original form is *tatadārakuhu* (present tense), because it is a future verb put in the subjunctive by the preceding light *an* (*an al-khafīfa*)." Some later scholars said: "This is not permissible as a narration of a past state, which requires [the verb to be read as] *tatadārakuhu*. Its meaning is: were it not for this present state, which was a blessing from God to him, he would have been cast out onto the barren land (*la-nubidha bil-ʿarāʾ*). A similar example is His words: ﴿and he found in them two men fighting﴾." The answer to *lawlā* (*lawlā*, "were it not for") is His words ﴿he would have been cast out onto the barren land﴾, which is blameworthy; that is, but He did not cast him out in a blameworthy state, as He said: ﴿so We cast him onto the barren land﴾. What is relied upon here is the circumstance, not casting out in absolute terms, but with the restriction of the circumstance. It was also said: "He would have been cast out onto the barren land of the Resurrection, blameworthy." This is indicated by His words: ﴿had he not been of those who glorify [God], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are raised﴾.

Then God informed that He ﴿chose him﴾ (*ijtabāhu*), that is, He selected him and made him among the righteous (*al-ṣāliḥīn*), that is, the prophets. From Ibn ʿAbbas: God returned the revelation to him and granted him intercession for his people.

When God commanded him to be patient with what He willed and forbade him from what He forbade, He informed him of the intensity of their enmity so that he would receive this with patience. He said: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you﴾, that is, they would almost make your people slip with their piercing gaze, which indicates extreme hostility; or they would destroy you, from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocked me down and almost devoured me," meaning: if his look had been able to knock down and devour, he would have done it. The poet said:

*They oppose one another when they meet in a battlefield,*
*with a look that would make the feet of the brave slip.*

Al-Kalbi said: *la-yuzliqūnaka* means *la-yaṣrifūnaka* ("they would turn you away"). The majority read ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*, from *azlaqa* (causative). Nafiʿ read it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, from *zalaqat al-rijl* ("the foot slipped"), transitivised by the *fatḥa* from *zalaqa al-rajul* with a *kasra*, like *shatarat ʿaynuhu* with a *kasra* and *shatarahā Allāh* with a *fatḥa*. ʿAbdullah, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿmash and ʿĪsā read ﴿la-yuzhiqūnaka﴾ (from *azhaqa*, "to destroy"). It was also said that the meaning of ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka bi-abṣārihim﴾ ("would slip you with their eyes") is: they would seize you by the evil eye (*al-ʿayn*). It is mentioned that bewitching by the evil eye (*al-laqf bil-ʿayn*) was found among the Banu Asad. Ibn al-Kalbi said: "A man among the Arabs would stay for two or three days without eating, then he would lift the side of his tent and say: 'I have never seen today camels or sheep more beautiful than these.' Then, not long after, a group or a number of them would perish." The disbelievers asked this man to strike the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he responded to them and recited:

*Your people used to consider you a leader,*
*and I think you are a leader who has been struck by the evil eye.*

That is, afflicted by the evil eye. So God protected His Prophet (ﷺ) and sent down this verse. Qatadah said: "It was revealed to repel the evil eye when they wanted to strike him with it, peace be upon him." Al-Ḥasan said: "The remedy for one afflicted by the evil eye is to recite this verse." Al-Qushayri said: "Affliction by the evil eye occurs only with admiration, not with dislike and hatred." He also said: ﴿and they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: "Disliking a thing does not prevent it from being afflicted by the evil eye out of enmity toward it, to the point of destruction." End of quote. It may be that the one who is struck by the evil eye, though hated by the one who strikes, has some quality that the striker admires, so he strikes him through that quality, especially if he possesses qualities of perfection.

﴿When they heard the Reminder﴾: whoever says that *lammā* ("when") is an adverbial clause whose governing element is ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka﴾, and even if it is a particle of obligation for obligation, which is the correct view, the answer is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: "When they heard the Reminder, they almost made you slip." The Reminder is the Qur'an. ﴿And they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾ to turn people away from him, though they knew that he (ﷺ) was the most complete of them in excellence and the soundest of them in intellect. ﴿And it is not but a reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an is nothing but admonition and lesson, ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, to jinn and humankind. So how can they attribute to jinn the one who brought it?

(p-315) When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that He had tested the disbelievers of Quraysh and compared their trial to the trial of the people of the garden, He informed them of the condition of their opposites, namely the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). He said: ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ He attributed the gardens to bliss (al-na'im) because bliss never leaves them, since nothing in them is except it, so it is not mixed with turbidity as the gardens of this world are mixed. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, Quraysh said: "If there is a garden there, we will have the greatest share in it." So it was revealed: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ Muqatil said: They said, "Allah has favoured us over you in this world, so He will favour us over you in the Hereafter; otherwise there is equal sharing." So He, the Exalted, answered: (﴿Shall We treat...﴾), meaning the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. This is an interrogative (istifham) containing a reproach and a rebuke for their error in what they said. Then He turned to them and said: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ "What is the matter with you" means: what is it with you concerning what you claim? This is an interrogative of denial directed at them. Then He said: "How do you judge?" This is a third interrogative in the manner of denial directed at them, asking about the manner of their judgment. In His saying "What is the matter with you" there is an inquiry about an undefined state, and in "How do you judge" there is an inquiry about the manner of their judgment.

Then He turned away from this to another matter, a transition (idrab intiqal) and not a cancellation of what came before, and said: ﴿Or do you have a Book in which you study?﴾ meaning: rather, do you have... (a Book) from Allah, (in which you study) that what you choose will be yours. The majority read ﴿Indeed for you therein is what you choose﴾ with a kasra on the hamza (inna). It was said that this is a resumption of speech, meaning: "If you have a Book, then you have therein a choice." It was also said: inna is the object of tadrusun (you study), meaning: you study in the Book that for you is what you choose, i.e., what you select of bliss. The hamza of inna was given a kasra because of the entering of the lam into the predicate, and it has the meaning of inna with a fatha on the hamza. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who began with it and said: "It is also permissible that it be a narration of what is studied as it is, like His saying: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations: Peace upon Nuh﴾ [al-Saffat: 78]." End of quotation. Talha and al-Dahhak read "anna lakum" with a fatha on the hamza, and the lam in lama is extra (za'ida), as it is in the reading of the one who read "illa annahum la-ya'kulun al-ta'am" with a fatha on the hamza of annahum. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum" as an interrogative.

﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us reaching to the Day of Resurrection?﴾ meaning: pledges (aqsam) binding upon Us, (reaching) meaning: extremely emphatic. It is said: "For so-and-so there is an oath upon me" when you swear to him to fulfil what you have sworn to. "To the Day of Resurrection" is connected to what the predicate is connected to, which is "for you", meaning: they are established for you until the Day of Resurrection; or it is connected to "reaching," meaning: they reach that day and end at it. The majority read "reaching" (balighah) in the nominative as an adjective, while al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "upon us." Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is a state from an indefinite noun, because it is specified, by way of predominance." ﴿Indeed for you is what you judge﴾ is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of "or do you have oaths upon Us" is: "or have We sworn to you?" This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum 'alayya," like the one before it, as an interrogative.

﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that﴾ meaning: who will be a guarantor (za'im) for what they say and claim to be true. "Ask" (sal) is suspended (mu'allaqah) from its second object. Since asking is a cause of acquiring knowledge, it is permissible to suspend it just as knowledge is suspended. Its second object originally would be governed by "an" or "bi," as Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and the poet said:

"If you ask me about women, then indeed I am knowledgeable of women's ailments, a physician."

If it had not been an interrogative, it would have been governed by "an" or "bi," as you say: "Ask Zayd about who looks into such-and-such." But he suspended "ask them," so the clause is in a place of accusative.

The majority read: ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ Abd Allah and Ibn Abi Ablah read "fa-l-ya'tu bi-shirkihim" (with their associate). It was said that in both readings the intended meaning is the idols, or people who share with them in their saying and agree with them in it, meaning: no one says what they say, just as they have no Book, no covenant from Allah, and no guarantor for this. So let them bring their partners. This is a summons and an inquiry. It was said: in this world, meaning let them bring them forth so that you see whether they are like those who harm and benefit or not. It was said: in the Hereafter, that they should bring them.

﴿On a Day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. According to this view, the one who governs the "day" is "let them bring." It was also said: remember (udhkur). It was also said the estimate is: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered, there will be such and such," and it was omitted for the great awe of what will happen in it of events. The apparent meaning, and the view of the majority, is that this Day is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim said: this Day is in this world, because He said: "and they will be called to prostration," and the Day of Resurrection contains no worship or obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is either the last days of a person's life in this world, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news﴾ [al-Furqan: 22], then he sees people called to prayer when its times come, but he cannot pray, because it is the time when faith will not benefit a soul. Or it refers to the state of illness, old age and infirmity. "And they used to be called to prostration before that day while they were sound," from what they now have. That is either because of the severity of the calamity upon them from the terror of what they witnessed at death, or from weakness and old age. It is answered that the calling to prostration is not by way of obligation, but by way of rebuke and humiliation. When they are called to prostration, they are deprived of the ability to do it, and power is withheld from them, so that their grief and regret over what they neglected when they were called to it, while their limbs and joints were sound, will increase.

The majority read "yukshafu" with a ya' in the passive voice. Abd Allah ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud also, and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a nun. Ibn Abbas read "yakshifu" with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. He also read it with a ya' with a damma in the passive voice. It was read "yukshifu" with a ya' with a damma and a kasra on the shin, from ak-shafa, when one enters into uncovering (kashf); from it: "ak-shafa al-rajul" meaning his upper lip retracted. The uncovering of the shin is a metaphor for the severity of the matter and its intensification. Mujahid said: it is the first hour of the Day of Resurrection, and it is the most terrible of them. What came in the hadith in His saying: "Then He will uncover for them the shin," is also to be understood as referring to severity on that Day, and it is a common metaphor in the language of the Arabs. Hatim said:

"A man of war, if war bites him, he bites it back, and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up as well."

And the rajaz poet said:

"I marvel at myself and at her concern, and at my chasing the horses from their provisions,
In a year that has uncovered its shin, red, stripping the flesh from its bones."

And the rajaz poet said:

"It has rolled up its shin, so tighten your grip; war has come upon you, so strive."

And another said:

"Patience before me, if evil remains; war has stood with us upon its shin."

And the poet said:

"It has uncovered its shin for them, and the calamities of evil have appeared."

It is also narrated as "al-Sudah." Ibn Abbas said: "on a Day when there is uncovering of a severe matter." Abu Ubaydah said: this is a word used for severity; it is said: "He uncovered his shin" when he rolled up his garment. He said: from this the Arabs say of a year of drought: "it has uncovered its shin." He made "shin" indefinite to indicate that it is an undefined matter of severity, outside the familiar, like His saying: ﴿On the Day when the caller calls to a thing unknown﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. It is as if it were said: "On a Day when a terrible, overwhelming matter occurs."

﴿And they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. Its apparent meaning is that they are called, and it has been mentioned that this is by way of rebuke, not by way of obligation. It was said: the caller is what they see of the prostration of believers, so they wish to prostrate but cannot, as occurs in the hadith in which Allah dialogues with them, that they say: "You are our Lord," and they fall down in prostration, so every believer prostrates, and the backs of the hypocrites and disbelievers become like cow-horns, one bone, so they are unable to prostrate. End of quotation. The negation of ability to prostrate in the Hereafter does not indicate that they have ability in this world, as al-Jubba'i held.

﴿Humbled (khashi'ah) their eyes﴾: a circumstantial state (hal), the subject of which is the pronoun in "they are called." He specified the eyes with humility, although all the limbs will be humble, because it is clearer in them than in every other limb. ﴿Humiliation will cover them (tarhaquhum)﴾ meaning: will overwhelm them, ﴿while they were being called to prostration﴾. It was said: this is an expression for all acts of obedience, and it was specified by mention because it is the greatest of acts of obedience, and because they were tested with it in the Hereafter. Al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi said: by prostration is meant the obligatory prayers. Ibn Jubayr said: they used to hear the call to prayer and "come to success," and they did not respond.

﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this message﴾. The meaning: leave Me to deal with him, for I will requite him, and there is no one to prevent Me. This is a severe threat to whoever denies what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought concerning the matter of the Hereafter and other things, and Allah, the Exalted, had already presented matters concerning the states of the happy and the wretched. "And whoever" (man) is in a place of accusative, either as a conjunction (ma'tuf) on the pronoun in "leave Me," or as an object with (maf'ul ma'ah). ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed My plan is firm﴾: it has been discussed in al-A'raf. ﴿Or do you ask them for payment, so they are burdened with debt﴾ up to ﴿write﴾: it has been discussed in al-Tur.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to invoke curse upon those who fled at Uhud when the matter became severe for the Muslims. It was also said: when he wanted to invoke curse upon Thaqif, and so this was revealed: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾, meaning: His granting them respite and delaying your victory over them, and proceed with what you were commanded of conveying the message and bearing harm. ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾: this is Yunus (peace be upon him), ﴿when he called out﴾, meaning: in the belly of the fish, and this is his saying: "There is no god but You; glory be to You." The prohibition is not directed at the persons themselves; rather the meaning is: let your condition not be like his condition. "When he called out": the governing element of "when" (idh) is the omitted noun to which it is attached, meaning: like the condition of, or like the story of, the companion of the fish when he called out. ﴿While he was suppressing (makzum)﴾: filled with anger against his people, since they did not believe when he invited them to faith, and they compelled him to hasten leaving them. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"And you, from love of Mayy, conceal a sorrow, afflicted in heart, anguished, suppressing, heavy in heart."

The root *k-ẓ-m* was already discussed in His words: ﴿and those who restrain their anger﴾. Most readers recite ﴿tadārakahu﴾ (his Lord's favour "reached" him) as a past-tense verb, without the feminine marker (*ta' al-ta'nīth*), in order to improve the separation between the verb and its subject. ʿAbdullah and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿tadārakathu﴾ with the feminine *tā'*. Ibn Hurmuz, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read it with a doubled *dāl* (*tadārrakahu*). Abu Hatim said: "This is not permissible. The original form is *tatadārakuhu* (present tense), because it is a future verb put in the subjunctive by the preceding light *an* (*an al-khafīfa*)." Some later scholars said: "This is not permissible as a narration of a past state, which requires [the verb to be read as] *tatadārakuhu*. Its meaning is: were it not for this present state, which was a blessing from God to him, he would have been cast out onto the barren land (*la-nubidha bil-ʿarāʾ*). A similar example is His words: ﴿and he found in them two men fighting﴾." The answer to *lawlā* (*lawlā*, "were it not for") is His words ﴿he would have been cast out onto the barren land﴾, which is blameworthy; that is, but He did not cast him out in a blameworthy state, as He said: ﴿so We cast him onto the barren land﴾. What is relied upon here is the circumstance, not casting out in absolute terms, but with the restriction of the circumstance. It was also said: "He would have been cast out onto the barren land of the Resurrection, blameworthy." This is indicated by His words: ﴿had he not been of those who glorify [God], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are raised﴾.

Then God informed that He ﴿chose him﴾ (*ijtabāhu*), that is, He selected him and made him among the righteous (*al-ṣāliḥīn*), that is, the prophets. From Ibn ʿAbbas: God returned the revelation to him and granted him intercession for his people.

When God commanded him to be patient with what He willed and forbade him from what He forbade, He informed him of the intensity of their enmity so that he would receive this with patience. He said: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you﴾, that is, they would almost make your people slip with their piercing gaze, which indicates extreme hostility; or they would destroy you, from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocked me down and almost devoured me," meaning: if his look had been able to knock down and devour, he would have done it. The poet said:

*They oppose one another when they meet in a battlefield,*
*with a look that would make the feet of the brave slip.*

Nafiʿ read it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, from *zalaqat al-rijl* ("the foot slipped"), transitivised by the *fatḥa* from *zalaqa al-rajul* with a *kasra*, like *shatarat ʿaynuhu* with a *kasra* and *shatarahā Allāh* with a *fatḥa*. ʿAbdullah, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿmash and ʿĪsā read ﴿la-yuzhiqūnaka﴾ (from *azhaqa*, "to destroy"). It was also said that the meaning of ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka bi-abṣārihim﴾ ("would slip you with their eyes") is: they would seize you by the evil eye (*al-ʿayn*). It is mentioned that bewitching by the evil eye (*al-laqf bil-ʿayn*) was found among the Banu Asad. Then, not long after, a group or a number of them would perish." The disbelievers asked this man to strike the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he responded to them and recited:

*Your people used to consider you a leader,*
*and I think you are a leader who has been struck by the evil eye.*

That is, afflicted by the evil eye. So God protected His Prophet (ﷺ) and sent down this verse. Qatadah said: "It was revealed to repel the evil eye when they wanted to strike him with it, peace be upon him." Al-Ḥasan said: "The remedy for one afflicted by the evil eye is to recite this verse." Al-Qushayri said: "Affliction by the evil eye occurs only with admiration, not with dislike and hatred." He also said: ﴿and they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: "Disliking a thing does not prevent it from being afflicted by the evil eye out of enmity toward it, to the point of destruction." End of quote. It may be that the one who is struck by the evil eye, though hated by the one who strikes, has some quality that the striker admires, so he strikes him through that quality, especially if he possesses qualities of perfection.

That is: "When they heard the Reminder, they almost made you slip." The Reminder is the Qur'an. ﴿And they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾ to turn people away from him, though they knew that he (ﷺ) was the most complete of them in excellence and the soundest of them in intellect. ﴿And it is not but a reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an is nothing but admonition and lesson, ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, to jinn and humankind. So how can they attribute to jinn the one who brought it?

(p-315) When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that He had tested the disbelievers of Quraysh and compared their trial to the trial of the people of the garden, He informed them of the condition of their opposites, namely the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). He said: ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ He attributed the gardens to bliss (al-na'im) because bliss never leaves them, since nothing in them is except it, so it is not mixed with turbidity as the gardens of this world are mixed. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, Quraysh said: "If there is a garden there, we will have the greatest share in it." So it was revealed: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ Muqatil said: They said, "Allah has favoured us over you in this world, so He will favour us over you in the Hereafter; otherwise there is equal sharing." So He, the Exalted, answered: (﴿Shall We treat...﴾), meaning the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. This is an interrogative (istifham) containing a reproach and a rebuke for their error in what they said. Then He turned to them and said: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ "What is the matter with you" means: what is it with you concerning what you claim? This is an interrogative of denial directed at them. Then He said: "How do you judge?" This is a third interrogative in the manner of denial directed at them, asking about the manner of their judgment. In His saying "What is the matter with you" there is an inquiry about an undefined state, and in "How do you judge" there is an inquiry about the manner of their judgment.

Then He turned away from this to another matter, a transition (idrab intiqal) and not a cancellation of what came before, and said: ﴿Or do you have a Book in which you study?﴾ meaning: rather, do you have... (a Book) from Allah, (in which you study) that what you choose will be yours. The majority read ﴿Indeed for you therein is what you choose﴾ with a kasra on the hamza (inna). It was said that this is a resumption of speech, meaning: "If you have a Book, then you have therein a choice." It was also said: inna is the object of tadrusun (you study), meaning: you study in the Book that for you is what you choose, i.e., what you select of bliss. The hamza of inna was given a kasra because of the entering of the lam into the predicate, and it has the meaning of inna with a fatha on the hamza. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who began with it and said: "It is also permissible that it be a narration of what is studied as it is, like His saying: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations: Peace upon Nuh﴾ [al-Saffat: 78]." End of quotation. Talha and al-Dahhak read "anna lakum" with a fatha on the hamza, and the lam in lama is extra (za'ida), as it is in the reading of the one who read "illa annahum la-ya'kulun al-ta'am" with a fatha on the hamza of annahum. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum" as an interrogative.

﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us reaching to the Day of Resurrection?﴾ meaning: pledges (aqsam) binding upon Us, (reaching) meaning: extremely emphatic. It is said: "For so-and-so there is an oath upon me" when you swear to him to fulfil what you have sworn to. "To the Day of Resurrection" is connected to what the predicate is connected to, which is "for you", meaning: they are established for you until the Day of Resurrection; or it is connected to "reaching," meaning: they reach that day and end at it. The majority read "reaching" (balighah) in the nominative as an adjective, while al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "upon us." Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is a state from an indefinite noun, because it is specified, by way of predominance." ﴿Indeed for you is what you judge﴾ is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of "or do you have oaths upon Us" is: "or have We sworn to you?" This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum 'alayya," like the one before it, as an interrogative.

﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that﴾ meaning: who will be a guarantor (za'im) for what they say and claim to be true. "Ask" (sal) is suspended (mu'allaqah) from its second object. Since asking is a cause of acquiring knowledge, it is permissible to suspend it just as knowledge is suspended. Its second object originally would be governed by "an" or "bi," as Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and the poet said:

"If you ask me about women, then indeed I am knowledgeable of women's ailments, a physician."

If it had not been an interrogative, it would have been governed by "an" or "bi," as you say: "Ask Zayd about who looks into such-and-such." But he suspended "ask them," so the clause is in a place of accusative.

The majority read: ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ Abd Allah and Ibn Abi Ablah read "fa-l-ya'tu bi-shirkihim" (with their associate). It was said that in both readings the intended meaning is the idols, or people who share with them in their saying and agree with them in it, meaning: no one says what they say, just as they have no Book, no covenant from Allah, and no guarantor for this. So let them bring their partners. This is a summons and an inquiry. It was said: in this world, meaning let them bring them forth so that you see whether they are like those who harm and benefit or not. It was said: in the Hereafter, that they should bring them.

﴿On a Day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. According to this view, the one who governs the "day" is "let them bring." It was also said: remember (udhkur). It was also said the estimate is: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered, there will be such and such," and it was omitted for the great awe of what will happen in it of events. The apparent meaning, and the view of the majority, is that this Day is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim said: this Day is in this world, because He said: "and they will be called to prostration," and the Day of Resurrection contains no worship or obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is either the last days of a person's life in this world, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news﴾ [al-Furqan: 22], then he sees people called to prayer when its times come, but he cannot pray, because it is the time when faith will not benefit a soul. Or it refers to the state of illness, old age and infirmity. "And they used to be called to prostration before that day while they were sound," from what they now have. That is either because of the severity of the calamity upon them from the terror of what they witnessed at death, or from weakness and old age. It is answered that the calling to prostration is not by way of obligation, but by way of rebuke and humiliation. When they are called to prostration, they are deprived of the ability to do it, and power is withheld from them, so that their grief and regret over what they neglected when they were called to it, while their limbs and joints were sound, will increase.

The majority read "yukshafu" with a ya' in the passive voice. Abd Allah ibn Abi Ablah read it with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud also, and Ibn Hurmuz read it with a nun. Ibn Abbas read "yakshifu" with a fatha on the ya' in the active voice. He also read it with a ya' with a damma in the passive voice. It was read "yukshifu" with a ya' with a damma and a kasra on the shin, from ak-shafa, when one enters into uncovering (kashf); from it: "ak-shafa al-rajul" meaning his upper lip retracted. The uncovering of the shin is a metaphor for the severity of the matter and its intensification. Mujahid said: it is the first hour of the Day of Resurrection, and it is the most terrible of them. What came in the hadith in His saying: "Then He will uncover for them the shin," is also to be understood as referring to severity on that Day, and it is a common metaphor in the language of the Arabs. Hatim said:

"A man of war, if war bites him, he bites it back, and if war rolls up its shin, he rolls up as well."

And the rajaz poet said:

"I marvel at myself and at her concern, and at my chasing the horses from their provisions,
In a year that has uncovered its shin, red, stripping the flesh from its bones."

And the rajaz poet said:

"It has rolled up its shin, so tighten your grip; war has come upon you, so strive."

And another said:

"Patience before me, if evil remains; war has stood with us upon its shin."

And the poet said:

"It has uncovered its shin for them, and the calamities of evil have appeared."

It is also narrated as "al-Sudah." Ibn Abbas said: "on a Day when there is uncovering of a severe matter." Abu Ubaydah said: this is a word used for severity; it is said: "He uncovered his shin" when he rolled up his garment. He said: from this the Arabs say of a year of drought: "it has uncovered its shin." He made "shin" indefinite to indicate that it is an undefined matter of severity, outside the familiar, like His saying: ﴿On the Day when the caller calls to a thing unknown﴾ [al-Qamar: 6]. It is as if it were said: "On a Day when a terrible, overwhelming matter occurs."

﴿And they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. Its apparent meaning is that they are called, and it has been mentioned that this is by way of rebuke, not by way of obligation. It was said: the caller is what they see of the prostration of believers, so they wish to prostrate but cannot, as occurs in the hadith in which Allah dialogues with them, that they say: "You are our Lord," and they fall down in prostration, so every believer prostrates, and the backs of the hypocrites and disbelievers become like cow-horns, one bone, so they are unable to prostrate. End of quotation. The negation of ability to prostrate in the Hereafter does not indicate that they have ability in this world, as al-Jubba'i held.

﴿Humbled (khashi'ah) their eyes﴾: a circumstantial state (hal), the subject of which is the pronoun in "they are called." He specified the eyes with humility, although all the limbs will be humble, because it is clearer in them than in every other limb. ﴿Humiliation will cover them (tarhaquhum)﴾ meaning: will overwhelm them, ﴿while they were being called to prostration﴾. It was said: this is an expression for all acts of obedience, and it was specified by mention because it is the greatest of acts of obedience, and because they were tested with it in the Hereafter. Al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi said: by prostration is meant the obligatory prayers. Ibn Jubayr said: they used to hear the call to prayer and "come to success," and they did not respond.

﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this message﴾. The meaning: leave Me to deal with him, for I will requite him, and there is no one to prevent Me. This is a severe threat to whoever denies what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought concerning the matter of the Hereafter and other things, and Allah, the Exalted, had already presented matters concerning the states of the happy and the wretched. "And whoever" (man) is in a place of accusative, either as a conjunction (ma'tuf) on the pronoun in "leave Me," or as an object with (maf'ul ma'ah). ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know﴾ up to His saying ﴿Indeed My plan is firm﴾: it has been discussed in al-A'raf. ﴿Or do you ask them for payment, so they are burdened with debt﴾ up to ﴿write﴾: it has been discussed in al-Tur.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to invoke curse upon those who fled at Uhud when the matter became severe for the Muslims. It was also said: when he wanted to invoke curse upon Thaqif, and so this was revealed: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾, meaning: His granting them respite and delaying your victory over them, and proceed with what you were commanded of conveying the message and bearing harm. ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾: this is Yunus (peace be upon him), ﴿when he called out﴾, meaning: in the belly of the fish, and this is his saying: "There is no god but You; glory be to You." The prohibition is not directed at the persons themselves; rather the meaning is: let your condition not be like his condition. "When he called out": the governing element of "when" (idh) is the omitted noun to which it is attached, meaning: like the condition of, or like the story of, the companion of the fish when he called out. ﴿While he was suppressing (makzum)﴾: filled with anger against his people, since they did not believe when he invited them to faith, and they compelled him to hasten leaving them. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"And you, from love of Mayy, conceal a sorrow, afflicted in heart, anguished, suppressing, heavy in heart."

The root *k-ẓ-m* was already discussed in His words: ﴿and those who restrain their anger﴾. Most readers recite ﴿tadārakahu﴾ (his Lord's favour "reached" him) as a past-tense verb, without the feminine marker (*ta' al-ta'nīth*), in order to improve the separation between the verb and its subject. ʿAbdullah and Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿tadārakathu﴾ with the feminine *tā'*. Ibn Hurmuz, al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash read it with a doubled *dāl* (*tadārrakahu*). Abu Hatim said: "This is not permissible. The original form is *tatadārakuhu* (present tense), because it is a future verb put in the subjunctive by the preceding light *an* (*an al-khafīfa*)." Some later scholars said: "This is not permissible as a narration of a past state, which requires [the verb to be read as] *tatadārakuhu*. Its meaning is: were it not for this present state, which was a blessing from God to him, he would have been cast out onto the barren land (*la-nubidha bil-ʿarāʾ*). A similar example is His words: ﴿and he found in them two men fighting﴾." The answer to *lawlā* (*lawlā*, "were it not for") is His words ﴿he would have been cast out onto the barren land﴾, which is blameworthy; that is, but He did not cast him out in a blameworthy state, as He said: ﴿so We cast him onto the barren land﴾. What is relied upon here is the circumstance, not casting out in absolute terms, but with the restriction of the circumstance. It was also said: "He would have been cast out onto the barren land of the Resurrection, blameworthy." This is indicated by His words: ﴿had he not been of those who glorify [God], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are raised﴾.

Then God informed that He ﴿chose him﴾ (*ijtabāhu*), that is, He selected him and made him among the righteous (*al-ṣāliḥīn*), that is, the prophets. From Ibn ʿAbbas: God returned the revelation to him and granted him intercession for his people.

When God commanded him to be patient with what He willed and forbade him from what He forbade, He informed him of the intensity of their enmity so that he would receive this with patience. He said: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you﴾, that is, they would almost make your people slip with their piercing gaze, which indicates extreme hostility; or they would destroy you, from their saying: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocked me down and almost devoured me," meaning: if his look had been able to knock down and devour, he would have done it. The poet said:

*They oppose one another when they meet in a battlefield,*
*with a look that would make the feet of the brave slip.*

Al-Kalbi said: *la-yuzliqūnaka* means *la-yaṣrifūnaka* ("they would turn you away"). The majority read ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*, from *azlaqa* (causative). Nafiʿ read it with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'*, from *zalaqat al-rijl* ("the foot slipped"), transitivised by the *fatḥa* from *zalaqa al-rajul* with a *kasra*, like *shatarat ʿaynuhu* with a *kasra* and *shatarahā Allāh* with a *fatḥa*. ʿAbdullah, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿmash and ʿĪsā read ﴿la-yuzhiqūnaka﴾ (from *azhaqa*, "to destroy"). It was also said that the meaning of ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka bi-abṣārihim﴾ ("would slip you with their eyes") is: they would seize you by the evil eye (*al-ʿayn*). It is mentioned that bewitching by the evil eye (*al-laqf bil-ʿayn*) was found among the Banu Asad. Ibn al-Kalbi said: "A man among the Arabs would stay for two or three days without eating, then he would lift the side of his tent and say: 'I have never seen today camels or sheep more beautiful than these.' Then, not long after, a group or a number of them would perish." The disbelievers asked this man to strike the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he responded to them and recited:

*Your people used to consider you a leader,*
*and I think you are a leader who has been struck by the evil eye.*

That is, afflicted by the evil eye. So God protected His Prophet (ﷺ) and sent down this verse. Qatadah said: "It was revealed to repel the evil eye when they wanted to strike him with it, peace be upon him." Al-Ḥasan said: "The remedy for one afflicted by the evil eye is to recite this verse." Al-Qushayri said: "Affliction by the evil eye occurs only with admiration, not with dislike and hatred." He also said: ﴿and they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: "Disliking a thing does not prevent it from being afflicted by the evil eye out of enmity toward it, to the point of destruction." End of quote. It may be that the one who is struck by the evil eye, though hated by the one who strikes, has some quality that the striker admires, so he strikes him through that quality, especially if he possesses qualities of perfection.

﴿When they heard the Reminder﴾: whoever says that *lammā* ("when") is an adverbial clause whose governing element is ﴿la-yuzliqūnaka﴾, and even if it is a particle of obligation for obligation, which is the correct view, the answer is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: "When they heard the Reminder, they almost made you slip." The Reminder is the Qur'an. ﴿And they say, "Indeed, he is a madman"﴾ to turn people away from him, though they knew that he (ﷺ) was the most complete of them in excellence and the soundest of them in intellect. ﴿And it is not but a reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an is nothing but admonition and lesson, ﴿to the worlds﴾, that is, to jinn and humankind. So how can they attribute to jinn the one who brought it?

(p-315) When Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that He had tested the disbelievers of Quraysh and compared their trial to the trial of the people of the garden, He informed them of the condition of their opposites, namely the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). He said: ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing with their Lord are gardens of bliss.﴾ He attributed the gardens to bliss (al-na'im) because bliss never leaves them, since nothing in them is except it, so it is not mixed with turbidity as the gardens of this world are mixed. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, Quraysh said: "If there is a garden there, we will have the greatest share in it." So it was revealed: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ Muqatil said: They said, "Allah has favoured us over you in this world, so He will favour us over you in the Hereafter; otherwise there is equal sharing." So He, the Exalted, answered: (﴿Shall We treat...﴾), meaning the obedient and the disobedient are not equal. This is an interrogative (istifham) containing a reproach and a rebuke for their error in what they said. Then He turned to them and said: ﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ "What is the matter with you" means: what is it with you concerning what you claim? This is an interrogative of denial directed at them. Then He said: "How do you judge?" This is a third interrogative in the manner of denial directed at them, asking about the manner of their judgment. In His saying "What is the matter with you" there is an inquiry about an undefined state, and in "How do you judge" there is an inquiry about the manner of their judgment.

Then He turned away from this to another matter, a transition (idrab intiqal) and not a cancellation of what came before, and said: ﴿Or do you have a Book in which you study?﴾ meaning: rather, do you have... (a Book) from Allah, (in which you study) that what you choose will be yours. The majority read ﴿Indeed for you therein is what you choose﴾ with a kasra on the hamza (inna). It was said that this is a resumption of speech, meaning: "If you have a Book, then you have therein a choice." It was also said: inna is the object of tadrusun (you study), meaning: you study in the Book that for you is what you choose, i.e., what you select of bliss. The hamza of inna was given a kasra because of the entering of the lam into the predicate, and it has the meaning of inna with a fatha on the hamza. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who began with it and said: "It is also permissible that it be a narration of what is studied as it is, like His saying: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations: Peace upon Nuh﴾ [al-Saffat: 78]." End of quotation. Talha and al-Dahhak read "anna lakum" with a fatha on the hamza, and the lam in lama is extra (za'ida), as it is in the reading of the one who read "illa annahum la-ya'kulun al-ta'am" with a fatha on the hamza of annahum. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum" as an interrogative.

﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us reaching to the Day of Resurrection?﴾ meaning: pledges (aqsam) binding upon Us, (reaching) meaning: extremely emphatic. It is said: "For so-and-so there is an oath upon me" when you swear to him to fulfil what you have sworn to. "To the Day of Resurrection" is connected to what the predicate is connected to, which is "for you", meaning: they are established for you until the Day of Resurrection; or it is connected to "reaching," meaning: they reach that day and end at it. The majority read "reaching" (balighah) in the nominative as an adjective, while al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read it in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in "upon us." Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is a state from an indefinite noun, because it is specified, by way of predominance." ﴿Indeed for you is what you judge﴾ is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of "or do you have oaths upon Us" is: "or have We sworn to you?" This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Al-A'raj read "a-inna lakum 'alayya," like the one before it, as an interrogative.

﴿Ask them which of them will guarantee that﴾ meaning: who will be a guarantor (za'im) for what they say and claim to be true. "Ask" (sal) is suspended (mu'allaqah) from its second object. Since asking is a cause of acquiring knowledge, it is permissible to suspend it just as knowledge is suspended. Its second object originally would be governed by "an" or "bi," as Allah said: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and the poet said:

"If you ask me about women, then indeed I am knowledgeable of women's ailments, a physician."

If it had not been an interrogative, it would have been governed by "an" or "bi," as you say: "Ask Zayd about who looks into such-and-such." But he suspended "ask them," so the clause is in a place of accusative.

The majority read: ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ Abd Allah and Ibn Abi Ablah read "fa-l-ya'tu bi-shirkihim" (with their associate). It was said that in both readings the intended meaning is the idols, or people who share with them in their saying and agree with them in it, meaning: no one says what they say, just as they have no Book, no covenant from Allah, and no guarantor for this. So let them bring their partners. This is a summons and an inquiry. It was said: in this world, meaning let them bring them forth so that you see whether they are like those who harm and benefit or not. It was said: in the Hereafter, that they should bring them.

﴿On a Day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration but they will not be able﴾. According to this view, the one who governs the "day" is "let them bring." It was also said: remember (udhkur). It was also said the estimate is: "On the Day when the shin is uncovered, there will be such and such," and it was omitted for the great awe of what will happen in it of events. The apparent meaning, and the view of the majority, is that this Day is the Day of Resurrection. Abu Muslim said: this Day is in this world, because He said: "and they will be called to prostration," and the Day of Resurrection contains no worship or obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is either the last days of a person's life in this world, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news﴾ [al-Furqan: 22], then he sees people called to prayer when its times come, but he cannot pray, because it is the time when faith will not benefit a soul.
